## Exploratory
(none)

## Literature note
The retrieved list is thin and largely off-topic for these hypotheses: none of the works examines misinformation sharing, perceived plausibility, source trust, tie strength, or conjoint (AMCE) designs, so prior findings on H1-H14, R1-R12 and X1-X13 cannot be summarized from it.

The only loosely relevant item is a review of prejudice and discrimination toward immigrants (Esses, 2020), which may bear indirectly on the sharer-origin hypotheses (H3, H10, X13), but its abstract snippet reports no findings about information sharing or credibility judgments, so we draw no conclusion from it. A substantive related-work section would require a new search targeting misinformation sharing, source cues, and conjoint survey experiments.

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis H/R with treatment arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference
level, so each estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level
instead of the reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control
group". Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with
that level that were chosen) between two respondent groups. If design.features shows that some features are respondents'
ratings of real people rather than randomized attributes, say once that their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts that bundle
correlated attributes, and keep causal language for the randomized feature. Lead with what the design is distinctive for.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-02 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint*

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-02; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

## Abstract

This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

## Key findings

- Profiles carrying misinformation were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Registered: close ties raised the chance a profile was chosen for sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003), and high sharer trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Registered: sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals roughly ±2 points.
- Exploratory, post hoc: among profiles chosen to share, misinformation was more often judged less plausible than the alternative post, 5.5 points above the true/neutral baseline (95% CI [3.0, 8.1]).
- Caveat: many tests were run without multiplicity correction, so borderline results (such as the moderate-sharer effect, p=0.034) should be read cautiously.

## Design and data

A conjoint with 7 profile features (Information type: True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check; Tie strength: Distant tie, Close tie; Sharer origin: Foreign origin, Continental US; Sharer ideology: Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; Trust in sharer: Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; Sharer political knowledge: Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; Sharer belief in disputed claims: Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent judged profiles built from seven randomized features, and the outcomes were whether a profile was chosen for sharing and whether it was chosen as more plausible. All 12,000 raw rows entered the analysis, though regressions used about 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility after missing values. The true/neutral reference level appeared in 4,145 profiles. Estimates are average marginal component effects against each feature's reference level, with standard errors clustered by respondent and two-sided p-values. Items labelled exploratory in the tables were specified after seeing the data and are post hoc.

## Results

### H1. Chosen to share

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Information type mattered most. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were also chosen less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Baseline sharing for true or neutral content was 60.3%.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

### H2. Chosen to share

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H2: effect by arm](figures/H2_arms.png)

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). The effect is modest but clearly positive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

### H3. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H3: effect by arm](figures/H3_arms.png)

Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points in sharing (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow, so only small effects in either direction are plausible, though the test cannot show there is none.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

### H4. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H4: effect by arm](figures/H4_arms.png)

Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034). Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) and not distinguishable from liberal ones. The moderate result is near the threshold and among many tests.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.019 | 0.009 | 0.0337 | [-0.037, -0.001] | 6538 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.007 | 0.011 | 0.5470 | [-0.028, 0.015] | 2536 | no |

### H5. Chosen to share

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H5: effect by arm](figures/H5_arms.png)

High-trust sharers were chosen 5.7 points more often than low-trust ones (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was +3.6 points (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]), suggestive but inconclusive. The low-trust level is the smallest group, with 817 profiles.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H5)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust: mid | 0.036 | 0.019 | 0.0561 | [-0.001, 0.073] | 2677 | no |
| Trust: high | 0.057 | 0.017 | 0.0010 | [0.023, 0.091] | 8388 | yes |

### H6. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on sharing: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H6: effect by arm](figures/H6_arms.png)

Mid and high sharer knowledge differed from low knowledge by −0.05 and +1.7 points in sharing. The high-knowledge interval was [−0.5, 3.9] points, so the data are inconclusive about effects of a few points.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H6)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.000 | 0.010 | 0.9619 | [-0.020, 0.019] | 5273 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1265 | [-0.005, 0.039] | 4564 | no |

### H7. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H7: effect by arm](figures/H7_arms.png)

A sharer believing disputed claims was chosen 0.2 points less often than one who did not (95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p=0.87). Effects larger than about 2 points are unlikely, but small ones cannot be excluded.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H7)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.002 | 0.009 | 0.8655 | [-0.019, 0.016] | 8675 | no |

### H8. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of information type on plausibility: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H8: effect by arm](figures/H8_arms.png)

Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less plausible than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p<0.001). Fact-checks were judged 12.4 points less plausible (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2]). Plausibility mirrors the sharing pattern.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H8)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.186 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.208, -0.164] | 3821 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.124 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.147, -0.102] | 3918 | yes |

### H9. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of tie strength on plausibility: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H9: effect by arm](figures/H9_arms.png)

Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p=0.008), close to the sharing effect.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H9)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.028 | 0.010 | 0.0079 | [0.007, 0.048] | 6664 | yes |

### H10. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer origin on plausibility: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H10: effect by arm](figures/H10_arms.png)

Continental US origin was −0.3 points on plausibility (95% CI [−1.9, 1.4], p=0.75), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H10)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | -0.003 | 0.008 | 0.7462 | [-0.019, 0.014] | 9402 | no |

### H11. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer ideology on plausibility: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H11: effect by arm](figures/H11_arms.png)

Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal ones (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p=0.026). Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), inconclusive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H11)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

### X5. Chosen to share

*A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls.*  
*Exploratory, not pre-registered.*

You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in research methodology.
Your task is to evaluate the methodological rigor of the paper sections provided.

Focus on:
- Study design appropriateness for the research questions
- Sample size and selection methodology
- Controls, baselines, and ablation studies
- Reproducibility (sufficient detail to replicate)
- Statistical methods and their appropriateness
- Potential confounds or threats to validity

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a specific software tool, model, or dataset
  exists). Focus ONLY on whether the methodology as described is rigorous and reproducible.
- If the paper acknowledges a limitation and provides a mitigation or robustness check,
  credit the authors for this rather than raising the issue as if unacknowledged.
- The text is a generated Markdown report. Tables are Markdown tables; the result tables
  appended after the sections are the source of every number in the prose.
- Be precise about what is missing vs. what is merely in a different section you may not have seen.
  If the paper says "see Appendix X" for details, note that rather than claiming the details are absent.
- When raising an issue, cite the specific number, table cell, equation, or passage
  you are questioning. For example: "In Section 4.2, the authors claim 15% but
  Table 3 shows 12.8%." Vague comments without concrete references are not useful.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)
  issue: string (short title of the issue, max 15 words)
  detail: string (detailed explanation of the problem)
  severity: string (one of: "critical", "major", "minor", "suggestion")
  suggestion: string (how to fix or improve)
  confidence: number (0.0 to 1.0, your confidence this is a real issue)

If you find no issues, return an empty array: []

CONTEXT FOR THIS REVIEW: the document is an AI-generated report of a survey experiment, produced from the authors'
data and pre-analysis plan. Analyses are tagged "registered" (as planned), "deviation" (planned, implemented
differently, with the reason stated) or "exploratory" (not planned). The plan is fixed: never ask for it to be
rewritten. Its multiple-testing policy is: none. If that policy is "none", it was the authors' choice;
you may note it as a limitation, but do not ask for corrections to be applied.

Add two keys to every object:
    kind: "analytical" when answering the issue needs a different or additional estimate (other covariates,
          estimator or standard errors, weights, a different sample or missing-data treatment, a robustness re-fit);
          "presentational" when only the prose, labels or tables need to change
    target: the hypothesis id the issue concerns (one of H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, H11, H12, H13, H14, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10, R11, R12, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7, X8, X9, X10, X11, X12, X13), or null

Paper: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
Abstract: This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

=== Sections to review ===
## Abstract
This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

## Key findings
- Profiles carrying misinformation were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Registered: close ties raised the chance a profile was chosen for sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003), and high sharer trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Registered: sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals roughly ±2 points.
- Exploratory, post hoc: among profiles chosen to share, misinformation was more often judged less plausible than the alternative post, 5.5 points above the true/neutral baseline (95% CI [3.0, 8.1]).
- Caveat: many tests were run without multiplicity correction, so borderline results (such as the moderate-sharer effect, p=0.034) should be read cautiously.

## Design and data
A conjoint with 7 profile features (Information type: True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check; Tie strength: Distant tie, Close tie; Sharer origin: Foreign origin, Continental US; Sharer ideology: Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; Trust in sharer: Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; Sharer political knowledge: Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; Sharer belief in disputed claims: Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent judged profiles built from seven randomized features, and the outcomes were whether a profile was chosen for sharing and whether it was chosen as more plausible. All 12,000 raw rows entered the analysis, though regressions used about 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility after missing values. The true/neutral reference level appeared in 4,145 profiles. Estimates are average marginal component effects against each feature's reference level, with standard errors clustered by respondent and two-sided p-values. Items labelled exploratory in the tables were specified after seeing the data and are post hoc.

## Results
### H1. Chosen to share

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Information type mattered most. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were also chosen less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Baseline sharing for true or neutral content was 60.3%.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

### H2. Chosen to share

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H2: effect by arm](figures/H2_arms.png)

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). The effect is modest but clearly positive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

### H3. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H3: effect by arm](figures/H3_arms.png)

Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points in sharing (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow, so only small effects in either direction are plausible, though the test cannot show there is none.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

### H4. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H4: effect by arm](figures/H4_arms.png)

Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034). Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) and not distinguishable from liberal ones. The moderate result is near the threshold and among many tests.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.019 | 0.009 | 0.0337 | [-0.037, -0.001] | 6538 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.007 | 0.011 | 0.5470 | [-0.028, 0.015] | 2536 | no |

### H5. Chosen to share

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H5: effect by arm](figures/H5_arms.png)

High-trust sharers were chosen 5.7 points more often than low-trust ones (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was +3.6 points (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]), suggestive but inconclusive. The low-trust level is the smallest group, with 817 profiles.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H5)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust: mid | 0.036 | 0.019 | 0.0561 | [-0.001, 0.073] | 2677 | no |
| Trust: high | 0.057 | 0.017 | 0.0010 | [0.023, 0.091] | 8388 | yes |

### H6. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on sharing: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H6: effect by arm](figures/H6_arms.png)

Mid and high sharer knowledge differed from low knowledge by −0.05 and +1.7 points in sharing. The high-knowledge interval was [−0.5, 3.9] points, so the data are inconclusive about effects of a few points.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H6)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.000 | 0.010 | 0.9619 | [-0.020, 0.019] | 5273 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1265 | [-0.005, 0.039] | 4564 | no |

### H7. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H7: effect by arm](figures/H7_arms.png)

A sharer believing disputed claims was chosen 0.2 points less often than one who did not (95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p=0.87). Effects larger than about 2 points are unlikely, but small ones cannot be excluded.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H7)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.002 | 0.009 | 0.8655 | [-0.019, 0.016] | 8675 | no |

### H8. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of information type on plausibility: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H8: effect by arm](figures/H8_arms.png)

Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less plausible than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p<0.001). Fact-checks were judged 12.4 points less plausible (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2]). Plausibility mirrors the sharing pattern.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H8)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.186 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.208, -0.164] | 3821 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.124 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.147, -0.102] | 3918 | yes |

### H9. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of tie strength on plausibility: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H9: effect by arm](figures/H9_arms.png)

Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p=0.008), close to the sharing effect.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H9)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.028 | 0.010 | 0.0079 | [0.007, 0.048] | 6664 | yes |

### H10. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer origin on plausibility: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H10: effect by arm](figures/H10_arms.png)

Continental US origin was −0.3 points on plausibility (95% CI [−1.9, 1.4], p=0.75), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H10)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | -0.003 | 0.008 | 0.7462 | [-0.019, 0.014] | 9402 | no |

### H11. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer ideology on plausibility: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H11: effect by arm](figures/H11_arms.png)

Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal ones (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p=0.026). Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), inconclusive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H11)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.021 | 0.009 | 0.0257 | [-0.040, -0.003] | 6539 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.019 | 0.011 | 0.0870 | [-0.041, 0.003] | 2537 | no |

### H12. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of trust in sharer on plausibility: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H12: effect by arm](figures/H12_arms.png)

Trust effects on plausibility were not distinguishable from zero: mid −0.6 points (95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]) and high +2.5 points (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]). Trust therefore shows clearer links to sharing than to plausibility.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H12)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust: mid | -0.006 | 0.018 | 0.7497 | [-0.042, 0.030] | 2675 | no |
| Trust: high | 0.025 | 0.017 | 0.1276 | [-0.007, 0.058] | 8392 | no |

### H13. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on plausibility: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H13: effect by arm](figures/H13_arms.png)

Sharer knowledge showed no distinguishable effect on plausibility; high knowledge was +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H13)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.001 | 0.010 | 0.9172 | [-0.021, 0.019] | 5271 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1188 | [-0.004, 0.038] | 4567 | no |

### H14. Chosen as more plausible

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on plausibility: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H14: effect by arm](figures/H14_arms.png)

Sharer belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.03 points, 95% CI [−1.8, 1.8]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H14)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.000 | 0.009 | 0.9700 | [-0.018, 0.018] | 8677 | no |

### R1. Chosen to share

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent; re-weighted by the inverse of the realized assignment probability of tie strength (stabilized).*  
*Pre-registered.*

![R1: effect by arm](figures/R1_arms.png)

With inverse-probability weights, the close-tie effect on sharing stayed at 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003), matching the unweighted result.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (R1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | weights = ipw_tie | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0033 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

### R2. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent; re-weighted by the inverse of the realized assignment probability of sharer origin (stabilized).*  
*Pre-registered.*

![R2: effect by arm](figures/R2_arms.png)

Weighted, continental US origin was +0.3 points for sharing (95% CI [−1.3, 1.9]), not distinguishable from zero and in line with the unweighted estimate.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (R2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | weights = ipw_origin | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | 0.003 | 0.008 | 0.7058 | [-0.013, 0.019] | 9400 | no |

### R3. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent; re-weighted by the inverse of the realized assignment probability of sharer ideology (stabilized).*

messages.content:
You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in statistical methodology and inference.
Your task is to evaluate the statistical reasoning, methods, and reported results in the paper.

Focus on:
- Hypothesis testing: Are one-sided vs two-sided tests used appropriately? Is the choice justified?
- Multiple comparisons: Are corrections (Bonferroni, FDR/q-values) applied when testing multiple hypotheses?
- Effect sizes and confidence intervals: Are they reported? Are they consistent with the test statistics?
- Wald ratios and test statistics: Verify arithmetic (e.g., does coefficient / SE = reported t or z statistic?)
- Sample size and statistical power: Is the sample adequate for the claimed effects?
- Causal language vs study design: Does the paper claim causation from observational/correlational designs?
- Robustness checks: Are sensitivity analyses appropriate and sufficient?
- Model assumptions: Are distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, independence) tested or discussed?

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- When raising an issue, cite the specific number, table cell, equation, or passage
  you are questioning. For example: "In Table 2, row 3: beta=0.47, SE=0.21, but
  0.47/0.21=2.24, not the reported t=2.89." Vague comments without concrete references
  are not useful.
- Do NOT focus on pure mathematical notation or derivation correctness — a separate
  math reviewer handles those.
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a cited statistical software or
  dataset exists). Focus on the internal validity of statistical reasoning.
- If the paper acknowledges a statistical limitation and provides a robustness check,
  credit the authors for this rather than raising it as if unaddressed.
- The text is a generated Markdown report. Tables are Markdown tables; the result tables
  appended after the sections are the source of every number in the prose.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)
  issue: string (short title of the issue, max 15 words)
  detail: string (detailed explanation of the problem)
  severity: string (one of: "critical", "major", "minor", "suggestion")
  suggestion: string (how to fix or improve)
  confidence: number (0.0 to 1.0, your confidence this is a real issue)

If you find no issues, return an empty array: []

CONTEXT FOR THIS REVIEW: the document is an AI-generated report of a survey experiment, produced from the authors'
data and pre-analysis plan. Analyses are tagged "registered" (as planned), "deviation" (planned, implemented
differently, with the reason stated) or "exploratory" (not planned). The plan is fixed: never ask for it to be
rewritten. Its multiple-testing policy is: none. If that policy is "none", it was the authors' choice;
you may note it as a limitation, but do not ask for corrections to be applied.

Add two keys to every object:
    kind: "analytical" when answering the issue needs a different or additional estimate (other covariates,
          estimator or standard errors, weights, a different sample or missing-data treatment, a robustness re-fit);
          "presentational" when only the prose, labels or tables need to change
    target: the hypothesis id the issue concerns (one of H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, H11, H12, H13, H14, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10, R11, R12, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7, X8, X9, X10, X11, X12, X13), or null

Paper: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
Abstract: This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

=== Sections to review ===
## Abstract
This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

## Key findings
- Profiles carrying misinformation were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Registered: close ties raised the chance a profile was chosen for sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003), and high sharer trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Registered: sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals roughly ±2 points.
- Exploratory, post hoc: among profiles chosen to share, misinformation was more often judged less plausible than the alternative post, 5.5 points above the true/neutral baseline (95% CI [3.0, 8.1]).
- Caveat: many tests were run without multiplicity correction, so borderline results (such as the moderate-sharer effect, p=0.034) should be read cautiously.

## Design and data
A conjoint with 7 profile features (Information type: True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check; Tie strength: Distant tie, Close tie; Sharer origin: Foreign origin, Continental US; Sharer ideology: Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; Trust in sharer: Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; Sharer political knowledge: Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; Sharer belief in disputed claims: Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent judged profiles built from seven randomized features, and the outcomes were whether a profile was chosen for sharing and whether it was chosen as more plausible. All 12,000 raw rows entered the analysis, though regressions used about 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility after missing values. The true/neutral reference level appeared in 4,145 profiles. Estimates are average marginal component effects against each feature's reference level, with standard errors clustered by respondent and two-sided p-values. Items labelled exploratory in the tables were specified after seeing the data and are post hoc.

## Results
### H1. Chosen to share

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Information type mattered most. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were also chosen less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Baseline sharing for true or neutral content was 60.3%.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

You are the handling editor for an automated review of a short research report on a survey experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Editorial guidance: at most 6 short, concrete instructions to the authors, most important first.
4. Unresolved questions: each phrased as a research question a follow-up study could answer, with why this study cannot, and the issue ids it came from.

Return:
{"assessment": "3-4 sentences: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and the single most important caveat",
 "claims": [{"claim": "short quote", "location": "Abstract|Key findings|H1|...", "verdict": "supported|overstated|unsupported", "evidence": "table and row, with the number", "fix": "rewording if not supported, else empty"}],
 "dispositions": [{"id": "R1", "disposition": "address|editorial|declined|unresolved", "reason": "one sentence"}],
 "editorial": ["..."],
 "unresolved": [{"question": "...", "why": "...", "from": ["R2"]}]}

## Registration
{"status": "registered", "url": "https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf", "note": "AsPredicted #132,508"}
Multiple-testing correction in the plan: none

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-02 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint*

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-02; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

## Abstract

This study asks which features of a shared post and its sharer shape whether people would pass it on and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov US sample of 12,000 profile judgments, respondents saw posts that varied in information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Misinformation was also judged 18.6 points less plausible. Close ties (+3.0 points, 95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high sharer trust (+5.7 points, 95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) increased sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Many tests were run without correction for multiple comparisons, so smaller effects should be treated cautiously.

## Key findings

- Profiles carrying misinformation were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Registered: close ties raised the chance a profile was chosen for sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003), and high sharer trust by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Registered: sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals roughly ±2 points.
- Exploratory, post hoc: among profiles chosen to share, misinformation was more often judged less plausible than the alternative post, 5.5 points above the true/neutral baseline (95% CI [3.0, 8.1]).
- Caveat: many tests were run without multiplicity correction, so borderline results (such as the moderate-sharer effect, p=0.034) should be read cautiously.

## Design and data

A conjoint with 7 profile features (Information type: True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check; Tie strength: Distant tie, Close tie; Sharer origin: Foreign origin, Continental US; Sharer ideology: Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; Trust in sharer: Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; Sharer political knowledge: Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; Sharer belief in disputed claims: Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Each respondent judged profiles built from seven randomized features, and the outcomes were whether a profile was chosen for sharing and whether it was chosen as more plausible. All 12,000 raw rows entered the analysis, though regressions used about 11,882 for sharing and 11,884 for plausibility after missing values. The true/neutral reference level appeared in 4,145 profiles. Estimates are average marginal component effects against each feature's reference level, with standard errors clustered by respondent and two-sided p-values. Items labelled exploratory in the tables were specified after seeing the data and are post hoc.

## Results

### H1. Chosen to share

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H1: effect by arm](figures/H1_arms.png)

Information type mattered most. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were also chosen less, by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). Baseline sharing for true or neutral content was 60.3%.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

### H2. Chosen to share

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H2: effect by arm](figures/H2_arms.png)

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). The effect is modest but clearly positive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

### H3. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H3: effect by arm](figures/H3_arms.png)

Continental US origin differed from foreign origin by 0.2 points in sharing (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow, so only small effects in either direction are plausible, though the test cannot show there is none.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

```

| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

### H4. Chosen to share

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H4: effect by arm](figures/H4_arms.png)

Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034). Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]) and not distinguishable from liberal ones. The moderate result is near the threshold and among many tests.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

### H5. Chosen to share

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

![H5: effect by arm](figures/H5_arms.png)

High-trust sharers were chosen 5.7 points more often than low-trust ones (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was +3.6 points (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3]), suggestive but inconclusive. The low-trust level is the smallest group, with 817 profiles.

messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

import importlib.util, pathlib
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = reg.HYPOTHESES
if isinstance(H, dict):
    h1 = H.get('H1') or [v for v in H.values() if v.get('id') == 'H1'][0]
else:
    h1 = [h for h in H if h.get('id') == 'H1' or h.get('analysis_id') == 'H1'][0]
est = h1['estimator']
cov = h1.get('covariates', [])
outcome = h1.get('outcome', 'share')

def run(sub):
    f, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, cov, sub)
    res = reg.fit(d2, f, est)
    out = {}
    for arm in ['Misinformation', 'Fact-check']:
        k = [t for t in res.params.index if 'T.' + arm in t and ':' not in t]
        out[arm] = (float(res.params[k[0]]), float(res.bse[k[0]]), int(res.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
o = run(df)
a = run(df[df.trial > 1])
for arm in o:
    rows.append(dict(arm=arm, est_orig=o[arm][0], se_orig=o[arm][1], n_orig=o[arm][2],
                     est_alt=a[arm][0], se_alt=a[arm][1], n_alt=a[arm][2]))
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv('results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)
print('E1 H1 drop trial1: ' + '; '.join(f"{r['arm']} {r['est_orig']:.3f}->{r['est_alt']:.3f} (se {r['se_orig']:.3f}->{r['se_alt']:.3f})" for r in rows))

rows2 = []
for lv in ['Lowest', 'Middle', 'Highest']:
    r = run(df[df.age_t == lv])
    for arm in r:
        rows2.append(dict(age_tertile=lv, arm=arm, estimate=r[arm][0], std_error=r[arm][1], n=r[arm][2]))
t = pd.DataFrame(rows2); t.to_csv('results/E2_h1_by_age.csv', index=False)
m = t[t.arm == 'Misinformation']
print('E2 misinfo AMCE by age tertile: ' + ', '.join(f"{x.age_tertile} {x.estimate:.3f}" for x in m.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(False)
for i, x in enumerate(m.itertuples()):
    ax.errorbar(x.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * x.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b', ecolor='#c0392b')
    ax.text(x.estimate, i + 0.2, x.age_tertile, ha='center', color='black')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel('Misinformation AMCE on sharing')
fig.savefig('figures/E2_age.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white', bbox_inches='tight')

You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = reg.HYPOTHESES
if isinstance(H, dict):
    h1 = H.get('H1') or [v for v in H.values() if v.get('id') == 'H1'][0]
else:
    h1 = [h for h in H if h.get('id') == 'H1' or h.get('analysis_id') == 'H1'][0]
est = h1['estimator']
cov = h1.get('covariates', [])
outcome = h1.get('outcome', 'share')

def run(sub):
    f, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, cov, sub)
    res = reg.fit(d2, f, est)
    out = {}
    for arm in ['Misinformation', 'Fact-check']:
        k = [t for t in res.params.index if 'T.' + arm in t and ':' not in t]
        out[arm] = (float(res.params[k[0]]), float(res.bse[k[0]]), int(res.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
o = run(df)
a = run(df[df.trial > 1])
for arm in o:
    rows.append(dict(arm=arm, est_orig=o[arm][0], se_orig=o[arm][1], n_orig=o[arm][2],
                     est_alt=a[arm][0], se_alt=a[arm][1], n_alt=a[arm][2]))
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv('results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)

print('E2 misinfo AMCE by age tertile: ' + ', '.join(f"{x.age_tertile} {x.estimate:.3f}" for x in m.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(False)
for i, x in enumerate(m.itertuples()):
    ax.errorbar(x.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * x.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b', ecolor='#c0392b')
    ax.text(x.estimate, i + 0.2, x.age_tertile, ha='center', color='black')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel('Misinformation AMCE on sharing')
fig.savefig('figures/E2_age.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white', bbox_inches='tight')
"}

Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = reg.HYPOTHESES
if isinstance(H, dict):
    h1 = H.get('H1') or [v for v in H.values() if v.get('id') == 'H1'][0]
else:
    h1 = [h for h in H if h.get('id') == 'H1' or h.get('analysis_id') == 'H1'][0]
est = h1['estimator']
cov = h1.get('covariates', [])
outcome = h1.get('outcome', 'share')

def run(sub):
    f, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, cov, sub)
    res = reg.fit(d2, f, est)
    out = {}
    for arm in ['Misinformation', 'Fact-check']:
        k = [t for t in res.params.index if 'T.' + arm in t and ':' not in t]
        out[arm] = (float(res.params[k[0]]), float(res.bse[k[0]]), int(res.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
o = run(df)
a = run(df[df.trial > 1])
for arm in o:
    rows.append(dict(arm=arm, est_orig=o[arm][0], se_orig=o[arm][1], n_orig=o[arm][2],
                     est_alt=a[arm][0], se_alt=a[arm][1], n_alt=a[arm][2]))
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv('results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)
print('E1 H1 drop trial1: ' + '; '.join(f"{r['arm']} {r['est_orig']:.3f}->{r['est_alt']:.3f} (se {r['se_orig']:.3f}->{r['se_alt']:.3f})" for r in rows))

rows2 = []
for lv in ['Lowest', 'Middle', 'Highest']:
    r = run(df[df.age_t == lv])
    for arm in r:
        rows2.append(dict(age_tertile=lv, arm=arm, estimate=r[arm][0], std_error=r[arm][1], n=r[arm][2]))
t = pd.DataFrame(rows2); t.to_csv('results/E2_h1_by_age.csv', index=False)
m = t[t.arm == 'Misinformation']
print('E2 misinfo AMCE by age tertile: ' + ', '.join(f"{x.age_tertile} {x.estimate:.3f}" for x in m.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(False)
for i, x in enumerate(m.itertuples()):
    ax.errorbar(x.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * x.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b', ecolor='#c0392b')
    ax.text(x.estimate, i + 0.2, x.age_tertile, ha='center', color='black')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel('Misinformation AMCE on sharing')
fig.savefig('figures/E2_age.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white', bbox_inches='tight')
"}

You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib

{"path": "scripts/04_exploratory.py", "content": "import importlib.util, pathlib
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = reg.HYPOTHESES
if isinstance(H, dict):
    h1 = H.get('H1') or [v for v in H.values() if v.get('id') == 'H1'][0]
else:
    h1 = [h for h in H if h.get('id') == 'H1' or h.get('analysis_id') == 'H1'][0]
est = h1['estimator']
cov = h1.get('covariates', [])
outcome = h1.get('outcome', 'share')

def run(sub):
    f, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, cov, sub)
    res = reg.fit(d2, f, est)
    out = {}
    for arm in ['Misinformation', 'Fact-check']:
        k = [t for t in res.params.index if 'T.' + arm in t and ':' not in t]
        out[arm] = (float(res.params[k[0]]), float(res.bse[k[0]]), int(res.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
o = run(df)
a = run(df[df.trial > 1])
for arm in o:
    rows.append(dict(arm=arm, est_orig=o[arm][0], se_orig=o[arm][1], n_orig=o[arm][2],
                     est_alt=a[arm][0], se_alt=a[arm][1], n_alt=a[arm][2]))
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv('results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)
print('E1 H1 drop trial1: ' + '; '.join(f"{r['arm']} {r['est_orig']:.3f}->{r['est_alt']:.3f} (se {r['se_orig']:.3f}->{r['se_alt']:.3f})" for r in rows))

rows2 = []
for lv in ['Lowest', 'Middle', 'Highest']:
    r = run(df[df.age_t == lv])
    for arm in r:
        rows2.append(dict(age_tertile=lv, arm=arm, estimate=r[arm][0], std_error=r[arm][1], n=r[arm][2]))
t = pd.DataFrame(rows2); t.to_csv('results/E2_h1_by_age.csv', index=False)
m = t[t.arm == 'Misinformation']
print('E2 misinfo AMCE by age tertile: ' + ', '.join(f"{x.age_tertile} {x.estimate:.3f}" for x in m.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(False)
for i, x in enumerate(m.itertuples()):
    ax.errorbar(x.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * x.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b', ecolor='#c0392b')
    ax.text(x.estimate, i + 0.2, x.age_tertile, ha='center', color='black')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel('Misinformation AMCE on sharing')
fig.savefig('figures/E2_age.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white', bbox_inches='tight')
"}

{"path": "scripts/04_exploratory.py", "content": "import importlib.util, pathlib
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = reg.HYPOTHESES
if isinstance(H, dict):
    h1 = H.get('H1') or [v for v in H.values() if v.get('id') == 'H1'][0]
else:
    h1 = [h for h in H if h.get('id') == 'H1' or h.get('analysis_id') == 'H1'][0]
est = h1['estimator']
cov = h1.get('covariates', [])
outcome = h1.get('outcome', 'share')

def run(sub):
    f, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, cov, sub)
    res = reg.fit(d2, f, est)
    out = {}
    for arm in ['Misinformation', 'Fact-check']:
        k = [t for t in res.params.index if 'T.' + arm in t and ':' not in t]
        out[arm] = (float(res.params[k[0]]), float(res.bse[k[0]]), int(res.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
o = run(df)
a = run(df[df.trial > 1])
for arm in o:
    rows.append(dict(arm=arm, est_orig=o[arm][0], se_orig=o[arm][1], n_orig=o[arm][2],
                     est_alt=a[arm][0], se_alt=a[arm][1], n_alt=a[arm][2]))
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv('results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)
print('E1 H1 drop trial1: ' + '; '.join(f"{r['arm']} {r['est_orig']:.3f}->{r['est_alt']:.3f} (se {r['se_orig']:.3f}->{r['se_alt']:.3f})" for r in rows))

rows2 = []
for lv in ['Lowest', 'Middle', 'Highest']:
    r = run(df[df.age_t == lv])
    for arm in r:
        rows2.append(dict(age_tertile=lv, arm=arm, estimate=r[arm][0], std_error=r[arm][1], n=r[arm][2]))
t = pd.DataFrame(rows2); t.to_csv('results/E2_h1_by_age.csv', index=False)
m = t[t.arm == 'Misinformation']
print('E2 misinfo AMCE by age tertile: ' + ', '.join(f"{x.age_tertile} {x.estimate:.3f}" for x in m.itertuples()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(False)
for i, x in enumerate(m.itertuples()):
    ax.errorbar(x.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * x.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b', ecolor='#c0392b')
    ax.text(x.estimate, i + 0.2, x.age_tertile, ha='center', color='black')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.8); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel('Misinformation AMCE on sharing')
fig.savefig('figures/E2_age.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white', bbox_inches='tight')
"}

value.title: H1 without trial 1
value.rationale: Checks whether the information-type effect on sharing depends on the first, possibly less attentive, trial.
value.method: Re-fit the registered H1 specification (OLS, cluster by respondent, same covariates) on trials 2-4, one arm against True/neutral at a time.
value.finding: The misinformation effect is -0.170 (SE 0.013) without trial 1, against -0.182 (SE 0.011) in the registered fit, so the result holds.

value.title: Misinformation effect by age tertile
value.rationale: Age is a demographic the PAP did not register, and it may change how much people penalise false content.
value.method: Re-fit the registered H1 specification within each age tertile.
