messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished survey experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures.

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

Return ONLY JSON:
{"takeaways": [str, ...], "abstract": str, "design_notes": str, "results": {"H1": str, "H2": str, "S1": str, ...}, "exploratory": {"E1": str, ...}, "limitations": str}

## Exploratory
- E1: H1 without trial 1 — The misinformation effect is -0.170 (SE 0.013) without trial 1, against -0.182 (SE 0.011) in the registered fit, so the result holds. [table results/E1_h1_drop_trial1.csv]
- E2: Misinformation effect by age tertile — The misinformation penalty on sharing is -0.130 in the youngest tertile and -0.220 in the oldest, so older respondents share it less. [table results/E2_h1_by_age.csv]

## Literature note
The retrieved list is thin and mostly off-topic for these hypotheses. It contains no experimental or survey findings on how information type, tie strength, sharer trust, ideology, knowledge or conspiracy belief affect sharing or perceived plausibility of misinformation, so it cannot support or contextualize H1-H14, the reweighted robustness checks R1-R12, or the exploratory analyses X1-X13. The only directly relevant item is a general review of fake news, disinformation and misinformation on social media [citation removed: not in retrieved set], whose snippet gives no specific findings. A review of prejudice toward immigrants (Esses, 2020) is only loosely related to the sharer-origin hypotheses (H3, H10, X13). Its snippet reports no findings on how sharer origin affects information sharing or credibility, so I draw no conclusions from it.

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-02 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint*

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-02; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.

## Key findings

- Headlines that were false or that corrected a false claim were shared less than true or neutral ones: misinformation by 18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), fact-checks by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]).
- Among the sharer attributes, which were measured and not randomized, a close tie raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±2 to ±4 points.
- Registered subgroup comparisons show that respondents with high belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with low belief (p<0.001), and older respondents shared it 6.1 points less.
- Many tests were run without correction, and the sharer attributes are measured ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive, not causal.

## Design and data

A conjoint with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

Each respondent rated pairs of posts, and the 12,000 profiles were all analysed; no rows were dropped for the main models, though a few outcome cells were missing by a handful of rows. Only the information type was randomized, with True/neutral headlines as the reference level (4,145 profiles with that level in the exploratory models). Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts. Their effects are therefore descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. All tests labelled registered follow the AsPredicted plan; those labelled exploratory were specified after seeing the data.

## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

False headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Sharing rates were 60.3% for true or neutral headlines, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. Because information type was randomized, these are causal estimates.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Posts from close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than those from distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). Tie strength is a measured rating, so the contrast is descriptive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

### H3. Sharer origin → sharing

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Posts from sharers in the continental US were not distinguishable from foreign-origin sharers in sharing (+0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow but still compatible with small effects either way.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

### H4. Sharer ideology → sharing

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034), a result near the threshold given the many tests. Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]), not distinguishable from liberal ones.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.019 | 0.009 | 0.0337 | [-0.037, -0.001] | 6538 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.007 | 0.011 | 0.5470 | [-0.028, 0.015] | 2536 | no |

### H5. Trust in sharer → sharing

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Highly trusted sharers were chosen 5.7 points more often than low-trust sharers (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was +3.6 points (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3], p=0.056), not clearly distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H5)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust: mid | 0.036 | 0.019 | 0.0561 | [-0.001, 0.073] | 2677 | no |
| Trust: high | 0.057 | 0.017 | 0.0010 | [0.023, 0.091] | 8388 | yes |

### H6. Sharer political knowledge → sharing

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on sharing: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Sharer political knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for sharing: mid knowledge −0.0 points (95% CI [−2.0, 1.9]) and high knowledge +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]), against low knowledge.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H6)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.000 | 0.010 | 0.9619 | [-0.020, 0.019] | 5273 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1265 | [-0.005, 0.039] | 4564 | no |

### H7. Sharer belief in disputed claims → sharing

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

High belief in disputed claims by the sharer was not distinguishable from low belief for sharing (−0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p=0.87).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H7)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.002 | 0.009 | 0.8655 | [-0.019, 0.016] | 8675 | no |

### H8. Information type → plausibility

*AMCE of information type on plausibility: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less often the more plausible post than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p<0.001).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H8)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.186 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.208, -0.164] | 3821 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.124 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.147, -0.102] | 3918 | yes |

### H9. Tie strength → plausibility

*AMCE of tie strength on plausibility: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points relative to distant ties (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p=0.008).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H9)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.028 | 0.010 | 0.0079 | [0.007, 0.048] | 6664 | yes |

### H10. Sharer origin → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer origin on plausibility: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.3 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.4]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H10)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | -0.003 | 0.008 | 0.7462 | [-0.019, 0.014] | 9402 | no |

### H11. Sharer ideology → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer ideology on plausibility: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal sharers (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p=0.026), near the threshold. Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H11)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.021 | 0.009 | 0.0257 | [-0.040, -0.003] | 6539 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.019 | 0.011 | 0.0870 | [-0.041, 0.003] | 2537 | no |

### H12. Trust in sharer → plausibility

*AMCE of trust in sharer on plausibility: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Trust in the sharer was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility: mid −0.6 points (95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]) and high +2.5 points (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H12)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trust: mid | -0.006 | 0.018 | 0.7497 | [-0.042, 0.030] | 2675 | no |
| Trust: high | 0.025 | 0.017 | 0.1276 | [-0.007, 0.058] | 8392 | no |

### H13. Sharer political knowledge → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on plausibility: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Sharer political knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility; high knowledge was +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]) and mid knowledge −0.1 points (95% CI [−2.1, 1.9]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H13)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.001 | 0.010 | 0.9172 | [-0.021, 0.019] | 5271 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1188 | [-0.004, 0.038] | 4567 | no |

### H14. Sharer belief in disputed claims → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on plausibility: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

The sharer's belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.0 points, 95% CI [−1.8, 1.8], p=0.97).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H14)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11884 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Arm | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (arm) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.000 | 0.009 | 0.9700 | [-0.018, 0.018] | 8677 | no |

### Re-weighted AMCEs: each source attribute re-weighted by its inverse assignment probability

*Pre-registered. Analyses R1–R12.*

Re-weighting each source attribute by its inverse assignment probability left the picture essentially unchanged. For sharing, close ties stayed at +3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust rose slightly to +6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The moderate-sharer contrast on sharing weakened to −1.7 points (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0], p=0.056). For plausibility, close ties (+2.7 points) and moderate sharers (−2.1 points) kept their sign and size. The remaining re-weighted estimates were not distinguishable from zero.

| Outcome | Feature | Level | Estimate | 95% CI | p | Without weights |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chosen to share | Tie strength | Close tie | 0.030 | [0.010, 0.050] | 0.003 | 0.030 (H2) |

You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in research methodology.
Your task is to evaluate the methodological rigor of the paper sections provided.

Focus on:
- Study design appropriateness for the research questions
- Sample size and selection methodology
- Controls, baselines, and ablation studies
- Reproducibility (sufficient detail to replicate)
- Statistical methods and their appropriateness
- Potential confounds or threats to validity

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a specific software tool, model, or dataset
  exists). Focus ONLY on whether the methodology as described is rigorous and reproducible.
- If the paper acknowledges a limitation and provides a mitigation or robustness check,
  credit the authors for this rather than raising the issue as if unacknowledged.
- The text is a generated Markdown report. Tables are Markdown tables; the result tables
  appended after the sections are the source of every number in the prose.
- Be precise about what is missing vs. what is merely in a different section you may not have seen.
  If the paper says "see Appendix X" for details, note that rather than claiming the details are absent.
- When raising an issue, cite the specific number, table cell, equation, or passage
  you are questioning. For example: "In Section 4.2, the authors claim 15% but
  Table 3 shows 12.8%." Vague comments without concrete references are not useful.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)

## Abstract
This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.

## Key findings
- Headlines that were false or that corrected a false claim were shared less than true or neutral ones: misinformation by 18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), fact-checks by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]).
- Among the sharer attributes, which were measured and not randomized, a close tie raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±2 to ±4 points.
- Registered subgroup comparisons show that respondents with high belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with low belief (p<0.001), and older respondents shared it 6.1 points less.
- Many tests were run without correction, and the sharer attributes are measured ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive, not causal.

## Design and data
A conjoint with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

Each respondent rated pairs of posts, and the 12,000 profiles were all analysed; no rows were dropped for the main models, though a few outcome cells were missing by a handful of rows. Only the information type was randomized, with True/neutral headlines as the reference level (4,145 profiles with that level in the exploratory models). Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts. Their effects are therefore descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. All tests labelled registered follow the AsPredicted plan; those labelled exploratory were specified after seeing the data.

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

False headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Sharing rates were 60.3% for true or neutral headlines, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. Because information type was randomized, these are causal estimates.

OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in statistical methodology and inference.
Your task is to evaluate the statistical reasoning, methods, and reported results in the paper.

Focus on:
- Hypothesis testing: Are one-sided vs two-sided tests used appropriately? Is the choice justified?
- Multiple comparisons: Are corrections (Bonferroni, FDR/q-values) applied when testing multiple hypotheses?
- Effect sizes and confidence intervals: Are they reported? Are they consistent with the test statistics?
- Wald ratios and test statistics: Verify arithmetic (e.g., does coefficient / SE = reported t or z statistic?)
- Sample size and statistical power: Is the sample adequate for the claimed effects?
- Causal language vs study design: Does the paper claim causation from observational/correlational designs?
- Robustness checks: Are sensitivity analyses appropriate and sufficient?
- Model assumptions: Are distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, independence) tested or discussed?

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- When raising an issue, cite the specific number, table cell, equation, or passage
  you are questioning. For example: "In Table 2, row 3: beta=0.47, SE=0.21, but
  0.47/0.21=2.24, not the reported t=2.89." Vague comments without concrete references
  are not useful.
- Do NOT focus on pure mathematical notation or derivation correctness — a separate
  math reviewer handles those.
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a cited statistical software or
  dataset exists). Focus on the internal validity of statistical reasoning.
- If the paper acknowledges a statistical limitation and provides a robustness check,
  credit the authors for this rather than raising it as if unaddressed.
- The text is a generated Markdown report. Tables are Markdown tables; the result tables
  appended after the sections are the source of every number in the prose.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)
  issue: string (short title of the issue, max 15 words)
  detail: string (detailed explanation of the problem)
  severity: string (one of: "critical", "major", "minor", "suggestion")
  suggestion: string (how to fix or improve)
  confidence: number (0.0 to 1.0, your confidence this is a real issue)

If you find no issues, return an empty array: []

CONTEXT FOR THIS REVIEW: the document is an AI-generated report of a survey experiment, produced from the authors'
data and pre-analysis plan. Analyses are tagged "registered" (as planned), "deviation" (planned, implemented
differently, with the reason stated) or "exploratory" (not planned). The plan is fixed: never ask for it to be
rewritten. Its multiple-testing policy is: none. If that policy is "none", it was the authors' choice;
you may note it as a limitation, but do not ask for corrections to be applied.

Add two keys to every object:
    kind: "analytical" when answering the issue needs a different or additional estimate (other covariates,
          estimator or standard errors, weights, a different sample or missing-data treatment, a robustness re-fit);
          "presentational" when only the prose, labels or tables need to change
    target: the hypothesis id the issue concerns (one of H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, H11, H12, H13, H14, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10, R11, R12, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7, X8, X9, X10, X11, X12, X13), or null

Paper: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
Abstract: This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.

=== Sections to review ===
## Abstract
This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.

## Key findings
- Headlines that were false or that corrected a false claim were shared less than true or neutral ones: misinformation by 18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), fact-checks by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]).
- Among the sharer attributes, which were measured and not randomized, a close tie raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±2 to ±4 points.
- Registered subgroup comparisons show that respondents with high belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with low belief (p<0.001), and older respondents shared it 6.1 points less.
- Many tests were run without correction, and the sharer attributes are measured ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive, not causal.

## Design and data
A conjoint with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

Each respondent rated pairs of posts, and the 12,000 profiles were all analysed; no rows were dropped for the main models, though a few outcome cells were missing by a handful of rows. Only the information type was randomized, with True/neutral headlines as the reference level (4,145 profiles with that level in the exploratory models). Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts. Their effects are therefore descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. All tests labelled registered follow the AsPredicted plan; those labelled exploratory were specified after seeing the data.

## Results
![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

False headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Sharing rates were 60.3% for true or neutral headlines, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. ### X1. A1. Trust in the sharer → sharing

*A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type.*  
*Exploratory, not pre-registered.*

Slope of Chosen to share on `trust_raw`: 0.014 (SE 0.004, p = 0.000, N = 11882). Significant at alpha = 0.05: yes.

Post hoc: each step up the 1-5 trust scale was linked to 1.4 points more sharing (SE 0.4, p<0.001). The slope was similar for misinformation (1.9 points) and fact-checks (1.7 points) and not clearly distinguishable from zero for true or neutral headlines (0.6 points).

You are the handling editor for an automated review of a short research report on a survey experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Editorial guidance: at most 6 short, concrete instructions to the authors, most important first.
4. Unresolved questions: each phrased as a research question a follow-up study could answer, with why this study cannot, and the issue ids it came from.

Return:
{"assessment": "3-4 sentences: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and the single most important caveat",
 "claims": [{"claim": "short quote", "location": "Abstract|Key findings|H1|...", "verdict": "supported|overstated|unsupported", "evidence": "table and row, with the number", "fix": "rewording if not supported, else empty"}],
 "dispositions": [{"id": "R1", "disposition": "address|editorial|declined|unresolved", "reason": "one sentence"}],
 "editorial": ["..."],

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-02 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint*

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-02; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

## Abstract

This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.

## Key findings

- Headlines that were false or that corrected a false claim were shared less than true or neutral ones: misinformation by 18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), fact-checks by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]).
- Among the sharer attributes, which were measured and not randomized, a close tie raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±2 to ±4 points.
- Registered subgroup comparisons show that respondents with high belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with low belief (p<0.001), and older respondents shared it 6.1 points less.
- Many tests were run without correction, and the sharer attributes are measured ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive, not causal.

## Design and data

A conjoint with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

Each respondent rated pairs of posts, and the 12,000 profiles were all analysed; no rows were dropped for the main models, though a few outcome cells were missing by a handful of rows. Only the information type was randomized, with True/neutral headlines as the reference level (4,145 profiles with that level in the exploratory models). Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts. Their effects are therefore descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. All tests labelled registered follow the AsPredicted plan; those labelled exploratory were specified after seeing the data.

## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

False headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Sharing rates were 60.3% for true or neutral headlines, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. Because information type was randomized, these are causal estimates.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Posts from close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than those from distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). Tie strength is a measured rating, so the contrast is descriptive.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

### H3. Sharer origin → sharing

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Posts from sharers in the continental US were not distinguishable from foreign-origin sharers in sharing (+0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow but still compatible with small effects either way.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034), a result near the threshold given the many tests. Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]), not distinguishable from liberal ones.

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

Slope of Chosen to share on `trust_raw`: 0.014 (SE 0.004, p = 0.000, N = 11882). Significant at alpha = 0.05: yes.

You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

- X1: A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type. (outcome share)
- X2: A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type. (outcome plausibility)
- X3: A1. The close-tie premium on sharing, net of the other source attributes, by information type. (outcome share)
- X4: A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. (outcome share_not_believe)
- X5: A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. (outcome share)
- X6: A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate. (outcome share)
- X7: B1. Message x respondent congruence: among partisan respondents shown partisan-slanted headlines, sharing of congenial against uncongenial content (headline slant from the paper's preliminary automated coding), by information type. (outcome share)

- X12: B3. Among misinformation profiles, the close-tie premium for health and political headlines. (outcome share)

messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

import importlib.util, pathlib
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('data/clean.csv')
H = {h['id']: h for h in reg.HYPOTHESES}

def run(hid, sub):
    h = H[hid]; est = h['estimator']; col = h['treatment']['column']
    out = {}
    for arm in h['treatment']['arms']:
        d = sub[sub[col].isin([arm, h['treatment']['control']])].copy()
        d['treat'] = (d[col] == arm).astype(int)
        covs = [c for c in est['covariates'] if c != col]
        need = [h['outcome'], est['cluster']] + covs + ([est['weights']] if est['weights'] else [])
        d = d.dropna(subset=need).reset_index(drop=True)
        e2 = dict(est); e2['covariates'] = covs
        f, d2 = reg.build_formula(h['outcome'], e2, covs, d)
        r = reg.fit(d2, f, e2)
        out[arm] = (r.params['treat'], r.bse['treat'], int(r.nobs))
    return out

rows = []
for hid in ['H1', 'H2', 'H5']:
    a = run(hid, df); b = run(hid, df[df.trial > 1])
    for k in a:
        rows.append(dict(hyp=hid, term=k, est_full=a[k][0], se_full=a[k][1], n_full=a[k][2],
                         est_alt=b[k][0], se_alt=b[k][1], n_alt=b[k][2]))
e1 = pd.DataFrame(rows); e1.to_csv('results/E1_drop_trial1.csv', index=False)
for _, m in e1.iterrows():
    print(f"E1 {m.hyp} {m.term}: full {m.est_full:.3f} ({m.se_full:.3f}) vs trials2-4 {m.est_alt:.3f} ({m.se_alt:.3f})")

rows = []
for tp in ['Health', 'Political']:
    a = run('H1', df[df.topic_type == tp])
    for k, v in a.items():
        rows.append(dict(topic=tp, term=k, estimate=v[0], std_error=v[1], n=v[2]))
e2 = pd.DataFrame(rows); e2.to_csv('results/E2_infotype_by_topic.csv', index=False)
for _, r in e2.iterrows():
    print(f"E2 {r.topic} {r.term}: {r.estimate:.3f} ({r.std_error:.3f}) n={r.n}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
for i, (_, r) in enumerate(e2.iterrows()):
    ax.errorbar(r.estimate, i, xerr=1.96 * r.std_error, fmt='o', color='#c0392b' if r.topic == 'Health' else '#222')
    ax.text(r.estimate, i + 0.25, f"{r.topic}: {r.term}", ha='center', fontsize=7)
ax.axvline(0, color='#222', lw=0.5); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel('Effect on sharing vs true/neutral')
for s in ['top', 'right', 'left']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('figures/E2_topic.png', dpi=200, facecolor='white')

- R12: AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on plausibility: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent; re-weighted by the inverse of the realized assignment probability of sharer belief in disputed claims (stabilized). (outcome plausibility)
- X1: A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type. (outcome share)
- X2: A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type. (outcome plausibility)
- X3: A1. The close-tie premium on sharing, net of the other source attributes, by information type. (outcome share)
- X4: A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. (outcome share_not_believe)
- X5: A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. (outcome share)
- X6: A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate. (outcome share)
- X7: B1. Message x respondent congruence: among partisan respondents shown partisan-slanted headlines, sharing of congenial against uncongenial content (headline slant from the paper's preliminary automated coding), by information type. (outcome share)
- X8: B2. A conspiracy-prone source: the slope of sharing on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims (0-1), net of the other source attributes, by information type. (outcome share)
- X9: B2. The slope of plausibility on the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims, by information type. (outcome plausibility)
- X10: B2, claim-specific (thin): for the anti-vaccine (polio) misinformation headline, plausibility when the sharer is seen as believing 'Covid-19 vaccines modify your DNA' against not. (outcome plausibility)
- X11: B3. Health vs. political misinformation: among misinformation profiles, the trust slope on sharing for health (guanabana, polio) and political headlines. (outcome share)
- X12: B3. Among misinformation profiles, the close-tie premium for health and political headlines. (outcome share)
- X13: B4. Sharer origin (continental US vs. elsewhere) and sharing, by survey language and by the respondent's nativity. (outcome share)

function.description: Hand a structured result to the orchestrator. Set final=true when your task is complete.

messages.content:
You are a quantitative social scientist adding a small set of EXPLORATORY analyses (at most three) to a survey experiment whose registered tests are already done. Choose analyses that help interpret the registered results: e.g. effects on component items, robustness to attention-check failures or alternative exclusions, heterogeneity by a demographic the PAP did not register, dose/manipulation checks, or a placebo. Avoid fishing; each analysis must have a one-sentence rationale.

Write ONE script scripts/04_exploratory.py (pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib Agg) that reads data/clean.csv, writes one tidy CSV per analysis to results/E<k>_<slug>.csv and at most two PNG figures to figures/ (minimal style: white background, no top/right/left spines, no gridlines, dark ink, one accent colour at most, direct labels instead of legends, 200 dpi), and prints one summary line per analysis. Use HC2 robust SEs. Run it with run_script; fix errors; then call
record_result(key="exploratory", value=[{"id":"E1","title":str,"rationale":str,"method":str,"table":"results/E1_x.csv","figure":"figures/..png" or null,"finding":one sentence with the key number}], final=true).
Reuse the registered script's helpers instead of writing your own model code. At the top of your script:
    import importlib.util, pathlib
    _spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('reg', pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('03_registered.py')); reg = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec); _spec.loader.exec_module(reg)
Then `formula, d2 = reg.build_formula(outcome, est, covariates, df_subset)` and `res = reg.fit(d2, formula, est)` give exactly the registered model (Lin centring, weights, HC2) on any subset; `reg.HYPOTHESES` holds each hypothesis dict with its `estimator` (use `est = h['estimator']`). For a plain weighted regression of your own, pass weights as a Series: `smf.wls(formula, data=d, weights=d['ipw']).fit(cov_type='HC2')` (never a column name string). Convert any object-typed numeric column with `pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce')` before fitting.
Robustness checks of a registered estimate must re-fit the SAME specification as scripts/03_registered.py (same formula, same weights column, same covariates and centring, same HC2 errors) on the alternative sample, and the table must hold both the original and the re-estimated estimate and SE side by side. If a standard error changes by more than a factor of two while the sample changes by less than 10%, your model is misspecified: fix it or drop the analysis.
Never print rows of data. Do not read data files directly.

You have 12 turns. Turn 1: write_file the full script. Turn 2: run_script. Fix and re-run if needed, then record_result with final=true. Record whatever analyses succeeded before you run out of turns.

- H1: AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent. (outcome share)

value.title: Information-type effect by health vs political topic
value.rationale: Health misinformation may be judged differently from political misinformation, so I checked whether the main AMCE depends on topic.
value.method: Registered H1 spec fit separately within Health and Political headlines; effects shown in a coefficient plot.
value.finding: Misinformation lowers sharing by 0.217 (SE 0.028) for health headlines and 0.176 (SE 0.012) for political headlines, so the penalty is similar in both and slightly larger for health.
