You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished conjoint experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures.

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

Return ONLY JSON:
{"takeaways": [str, ...], "abstract": str, "design_notes": str, "results": {"H1": str, "H2": str, "S1": str, ...}, "exploratory": {"E1": str, ...}, "limitations": str}

- X5 [exploratory]: A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. (outcome share, direction two_sided)
- X6 [exploratory]: A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. (outcome share, direction two_sided)

## Exploratory
- E1: Robustness: drop trial 1 — Misinformation AMCE on sharing is -0.182 (SE 0.011) in the full sample and -0.170 (SE 0.013) without trial 1, and the trust-high effect is 0.058 vs 0.066, so the registered results hold. [table results/E1_drop_trial1.csv]
- E2: Information-type effect by health vs political topic — Misinformation lowers sharing by 0.217 (SE 0.028) for health headlines and 0.176 (SE 0.012) for political headlines, so the penalty is similar in both and slightly larger for health. [table results/E2_infotype_by_topic.csv]

## Literature note
The retrieved list is thin and largely off-topic: none of the ten works reports findings on how information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge, or conspiracy belief affect sharing or plausibility judgments of misinformation. The 'supporting' items are broad overviews (Van Bavel et al., 2020; Dwivedi et al., 2019; Jenkins & Purushotma, 2006) with no abstract text bearing on the hypotheses, so they cannot be read as evidence for any of H1-H14. The closest topical neighbors are the conjoint study of deceitful political behavior and political trust [citation removed: not in retrieved set] and the work on political lies and election-loss acceptance (Arceneaux & Truex, 2022). Both concern political deception and trust rather than sharing decisions, so they are context at most. The conjoint design of Christensen et al. (2025) is the only item that resembles the study's method.

The works do not disagree with each other or with the study's expectations on any substantive question about sharing or plausibility. The 'contesting' items (Chater & Loewenstein, 2022, in two versions; Sutton et al., 2010) address individual-level framing of behavioral policy and distributed memory, and they do not test the hypothesized effects. Because no retrieved work reports findings on these questions, the study's design cannot be said to adjudicate between any of them. The abstract for Nativist disidentification (López Ortega & Turnbull-Dugarte, 2025) mentions out-group signals, which is only loosely related to the origin hypotheses (H3, H10), and the snippet is too brief to support a comparison.

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-03 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: unreviewed](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #132,508](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: conjoint](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-03; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it affect whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing, while a moderate sharer lowered it by 1.9 points. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Plausibility judgments followed a similar pattern. Sharer traits are measured rather than randomized, so these are descriptive contrasts, and many tests were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Among the measured sharer attributes, high trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of about ±2 to 4 points.
- Registered subgroup tests show misinformation was shared more by respondents who believe more disputed claims, by 5.6 points (SE 0.017); true or neutral items were shared less by them.
- Only information type is randomized; the sharer attributes are measured contrasts. The many tests are uncorrected, and the exploratory analyses are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). All 12,000 profile ratings were analysed, with small losses from missing values in some models (for example 3,854 eligible misinformation profiles, 3,822 used). The control level, true or neutral headlines, had about 4,100 profiles. Only the information type of the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was shared 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p<0.001). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Information type is the randomized feature, so these are causal estimates.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in research methodology.
Your task is to evaluate the methodological rigor of the paper sections provided.

Focus on:
- Study design appropriateness for the research questions
- Sample size and selection methodology
- Controls, baselines, and ablation studies

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a specific software tool, model, or dataset

- If the paper acknowledges a limitation and provides a mitigation or robustness check,

  you are questioning. For example: "In Section 4.2, the authors claim 15% but
  Table 3 shows 12.8%." Vague comments without concrete references are not useful.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)
  issue: string (short title of the issue, max 15 words)
  detail: string (detailed explanation of the problem)
  severity: string (one of: "critical", "major", "minor", "suggestion")

If you find no issues, return an empty array: []

CONTEXT FOR THIS REVIEW: the document is an AI-generated report of a conjoint experiment, produced from the authors'
data and pre-analysis plan. Analyses are tagged "registered" (as planned), "deviation" (planned, implemented
differently, with the reason stated) or "exploratory" (not planned). The plan is fixed: never ask for it to be
rewritten. Its multiple-testing policy is: none. If that policy is "none", it was the authors' choice;
you may note it as a limitation, but do not ask for corrections to be applied.

Add two keys to every object:
    kind: "analytical" when answering the issue needs a different or additional estimate (other covariates,
          estimator or standard errors, weights, a different sample or missing-data treatment, a robustness re-fit);
          "presentational" when only the prose, labels or tables need to change
    target: the hypothesis id the issue concerns (one of H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, H11, H12, H13, H14, R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10, R11, R12, X1, X2, X3, X4, X5, X6, X7, X8, X9, X10, X11, X12, X13), or null

Paper: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
Abstract: We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it affect whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing, while a moderate sharer lowered it by 1.9 points. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Plausibility judgments followed a similar pattern. Sharer traits are measured rather than randomized, so these are descriptive contrasts, and many tests were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->

=== Sections to review ===
## Abstract
We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it affect whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing, while a moderate sharer lowered it by 1.9 points. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Plausibility judgments followed a similar pattern. Sharer traits are measured rather than randomized, so these are descriptive contrasts, and many tests were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->

## Key findings
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Among the measured sharer attributes, high trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of about ±2 to 4 points.
- Registered subgroup tests show misinformation was shared more by respondents who believe more disputed claims, by 5.6 points (SE 0.017); true or neutral items were shared less by them.
- Only information type is randomized; the sharer attributes are measured contrasts. The many tests are uncorrected, and the exploratory analyses are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->

## Design and data
A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). All 12,000 profile ratings were analysed, with small losses from missing values in some models (for example 3,854 eligible misinformation profiles, 3,822 used). The control level, true or neutral headlines, had about 4,100 profiles. Only the information type of the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->

## Results
![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was shared 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p<0.001). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Information type is the randomized feature, so these are causal estimates.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H2 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p=0.003). This is a measured contrast, not a randomized one.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H3 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H3. Sharer origin → sharing

*AMCE of sharer origin on sharing: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Continental US sharers were shared 0.2 points more often than foreign-origin sharers (95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). This is not distinguishable from zero and rules out only large effects.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H3)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Continental US | 0.002 | 0.008 | 0.8143 | [-0.014, 0.018] | 9400 | no |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H4 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H4. Sharer ideology → sharing

*AMCE of sharer ideology on sharing: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Moderate sharers were shared 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034), a result near the threshold. Conservative sharers differed by −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H4)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Level | Estimate | SE | p | 95% CI | n (level) | Supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Moderate sharer | -0.019 | 0.009 | 0.0337 | [-0.037, -0.001] | 6538 | yes |
| Conservative sharer | -0.007 | 0.011 | 0.5470 | [-0.028, 0.015] | 2536 | no |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H5 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H5. Trust in sharer → sharing

*AMCE of trust in sharer on sharing: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

High-trust sharers were shared 5.7 points more often than low-trust ones (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was 3.6 points higher (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3], p=0.056), not clearly separable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H5)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

| Trust: high | 0.057 | 0.017 | 0.0010 | [0.023, 0.091] | 8388 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H6 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H6. Sharer political knowledge → sharing

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on sharing: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Mid and high political knowledge differed from low knowledge by −0.0 and +1.7 points. The high-knowledge interval ran from −0.5 to 3.9 points, so neither level was distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H6)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Knowledge: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge: mid | -0.000 | 0.010 | 0.9619 | [-0.020, 0.019] | 5273 | no |
| Knowledge: high | 0.017 | 0.011 | 0.1265 | [-0.005, 0.039] | 4564 | no |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H7 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H7. Sharer belief in disputed claims → sharing

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on sharing: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Sharers with high belief in disputed claims were shared 0.2 points less often than those with low belief (95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p=0.87). This is not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H7)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Conspiracy belief: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge)

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conspiracy belief: high | -0.002 | 0.009 | 0.8655 | [-0.019, 0.016] | 8675 | no |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H8 tag=registered outcome=plausibility -->
### H8. Information type → plausibility

*AMCE of information type on plausibility: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less plausible than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p<0.001). Fact-checks were 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p<0.001).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H8)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.186 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.208, -0.164] | 3821 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.124 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.147, -0.102] | 3918 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H9 tag=registered outcome=plausibility -->
### H9. Tie strength → plausibility

*AMCE of tie strength on plausibility: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], two-sided p=0.008). This is a measured contrast.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H9)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H10 tag=registered outcome=plausibility -->
### H10. Sharer origin → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer origin on plausibility: each level against 'Foreign origin', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Continental US origin changed plausibility by −0.3 points (95% CI [−1.9, 1.4], p=0.75), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H10)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Foreign origin')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

*AMCE of sharer ideology on plausibility: each level against 'Liberal sharer', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal sharers (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p=0.026), near the threshold. Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H11)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Liberal sharer')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

```

### H12. Trust in sharer → plausibility

*AMCE of trust in sharer on plausibility: each level against 'Trust: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Trust in the sharer was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High trust was +2.5 points (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]) and mid trust −0.6 points (95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]).

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H12)

```
plausibility ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Trust: low')) + C(infotype) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

*AMCE of sharer political knowledge on plausibility: each level against 'Knowledge: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Sharer knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility. High knowledge was +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]) and mid knowledge −0.1 points.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H13)

### H14. Sharer belief in disputed claims → plausibility

*AMCE of sharer belief in disputed claims on plausibility: each level against 'Conspiracy belief: low', from the regression of plausibility on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*

<!-- fd:group id=RW -->
### Re-weighted AMCEs: each source attribute re-weighted by its inverse assignment probability

*Pre-registered. Analyses R1–R12.*

Re-weighting each sharer attribute by its inverse assignment probability gave estimates very close to the unweighted ones. Close ties still raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust by 6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). messages.content:
You are a senior academic reviewer specializing in statistical methodology and inference.
Your task is to evaluate the statistical reasoning, methods, and reported results in the paper.

Focus on:
- Hypothesis testing: Are one-sided vs two-sided tests used appropriately? Is the choice justified?
- Multiple comparisons: Are corrections (Bonferroni, FDR/q-values) applied when testing multiple hypotheses?
- Effect sizes and confidence intervals: Are they reported? Are they consistent with the test statistics?
- Wald ratios and test statistics: Verify arithmetic (e.g., does coefficient / SE = reported t or z statistic?)
- Sample size and statistical power: Is the sample adequate for the claimed effects?
- Causal language vs study design: Does the paper claim causation from observational/correlational designs?
- Robustness checks: Are sensitivity analyses appropriate and sufficient?
- Model assumptions: Are distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, independence) tested or discussed?

IMPORTANT GUIDELINES:
- When raising an issue, cite the specific number, table cell, equation, or passage
  you are questioning. For example: "In Table 2, row 3: beta=0.47, SE=0.21, but
  0.47/0.21=2.24, not the reported t=2.89." Vague comments without concrete references
  are not useful.
- Do NOT focus on pure mathematical notation or derivation correctness — a separate
  math reviewer handles those.
- Do NOT fact-check external claims (e.g., whether a cited statistical software or
  dataset exists). Focus on the internal validity of statistical reasoning.
- If the paper acknowledges a statistical limitation and provides a robustness check,
  credit the authors for this rather than raising it as if unaddressed.
- The text is a generated Markdown report. Tables are Markdown tables; the result tables
  appended after the sections are the source of every number in the prose.

Respond ONLY with a JSON array of objects. Each object must have these keys:
  section_ref: string (which section the issue is in)
  issue: string (short title of the issue, max 15 words)
  detail: string (detailed explanation of the problem)
  severity: string (one of: "critical", "major", "minor", "suggestion")
  suggestion: string (how to fix or improve)
  confidence: number (0.0 to 1.0, your confidence this is a real issue)

If you find no issues, return an empty array: []

CONTEXT FOR THIS REVIEW: the document is an AI-generated report of a conjoint experiment, produced from the authors'
data and pre-analysis plan. Analyses are tagged "registered" (as planned), "deviation" (planned, implemented
differently, with the reason stated) or "exploratory" (not planned). The plan is fixed: never ask for it to be
rewritten. Its multiple-testing policy is: none. If that policy is "none", it was the authors' choice;
you may note it as a limitation, but do not ask for corrections to be applied.

Add two keys to every object:

## Abstract
We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it affect whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing, while a moderate sharer lowered it by 1.9 points. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Plausibility judgments followed a similar pattern. Sharer traits are measured rather than randomized, so these are descriptive contrasts, and many tests were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->

## Key findings
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Among the measured sharer attributes, high trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of about ±2 to 4 points.
- Registered subgroup tests show misinformation was shared more by respondents who believe more disputed claims, by 5.6 points (SE 0.017); true or neutral items were shared less by them.
- Only information type is randomized; the sharer attributes are measured contrasts. The many tests are uncorrected, and the exploratory analyses are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->

## Design and data
A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). All 12,000 profile ratings were analysed, with small losses from missing values in some models (for example 3,854 eligible misinformation profiles, 3,822 used). The control level, true or neutral headlines, had about 4,100 profiles. Only the information type of the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

You are the handling editor for an automated review of a short research report on a conjoint experiment. You receive the report, its result tables, the registration status of its analysis plan, and the issues raised by one or more automated reviewers. You do four things and return ONLY JSON.

1. Pressure-test claims. Find every quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12, the most consequential first). For each, check it against the tables: the number, its sign, its interval, the outcome it is about, and whether the wording (e.g. "improved", "the only arm", "no effect") is justified. Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables).
2. Give every reviewer issue a disposition:
   - "address": a different or additional estimate on the same data would answer it (covariates, estimator, weights, sample, a robustness re-fit);
   - "editorial": only prose, labels, tables or missing detail need fixing;
   - "declined": answering it would change the pre-registered analysis (for example, a multiple-testing correction the plan does not specify, a different primary outcome). Say which part of the plan it conflicts with. Registered analyses are never changed to satisfy a reviewer;
   - "unresolved": the data cannot settle it (needs a new sample, a different design, a measure that was not collected), or reviewers disagree in a way the tables cannot resolve.
3. Editorial guidance: at most 6 short, concrete instructions to the authors, most important first.
4. Unresolved questions: each phrased as a research question a follow-up study could answer, with why this study cannot, and the issue ids it came from.

Return:
{"assessment": "3-4 sentences: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and the single most important caveat",
 "claims": [{"claim": "short quote", "location": "Abstract|Key findings|H1|...", "verdict": "supported|overstated|unsupported", "evidence": "table and row, with the number", "fix": "rewording if not supported, else empty"}],

## Registration
{"status": "registered", "url": "https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf", "note": "AsPredicted #132,508"}
Multiple-testing correction in the plan: none

## Design
A conjoint experiment; causal design: yes; respondents: human.

## Report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-03 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: unreviewed](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #132,508](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: conjoint](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-03; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: no. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it affect whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), and fact-checks 13.3 points less often. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing, while a moderate sharer lowered it by 1.9 points. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Plausibility judgments followed a similar pattern. Sharer traits are measured rather than randomized, so these are descriptive contrasts, and many tests were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were also shared less, by 13.3 points.
- Among the measured sharer attributes, high trust in the sharer raised sharing by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]).
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of about ±2 to 4 points.
- Registered subgroup tests show misinformation was shared more by respondents who believe more disputed claims, by 5.6 points (SE 0.017); true or neutral items were shared less by them.
- Only information type is randomized; the sharer attributes are measured contrasts. The many tests are uncorrected, and the exploratory analyses are post hoc.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). All 12,000 profile ratings were analysed, with small losses from missing values in some models (for example 3,854 eligible misinformation profiles, 3,822 used). The control level, true or neutral headlines, had about 4,100 profiles. Only the information type of the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent.

<!-- fd:section id=results -->
## Results

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen to share (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_share.png)

![Effects of every profile feature on chosen as more plausible (AMCEs, 95% CI)](figures/amce_plausibility.png)

<!-- fd:hyp id=H1 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H1. Information type → sharing

*AMCE of information type on sharing: each level against 'True/neutral', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Misinformation was shared 18.2 points less often than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], two-sided p<0.001). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Information type is the randomized feature, so these are causal estimates.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H1)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='True/neutral')) + C(tie) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)
OLS | cluster-robust SEs on resp_id | N = 11882 | two-sided test, alpha = 0.05
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Misinformation | -0.182 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.204, -0.160] | 3822 | yes |
| Fact-check | -0.133 | 0.011 | < 0.0001 | [-0.156, -0.111] | 3915 | yes |

<!-- fd:hyp id=H2 tag=registered outcome=share -->
### H2. Tie strength → sharing

*AMCE of tie strength on sharing: each level against 'Distant tie', from the regression of sharing on all seven profile features, SEs clustered by respondent.*  
*Pre-registered.*

Close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], two-sided p=0.003). This is a measured contrast, not a randomized one.

#### Details: model and estimates by arm (H2)

```
share ~ C(arm_code, Treatment(reference='Distant tie')) + C(infotype) + C(sharer_origin) + C(sharer_ideology) + C(sharer_trust) + C(sharer_knowledge) + C(sharer_conspiracy)

| Close tie | 0.030 | 0.010 | 0.0032 | [0.010, 0.050] | 6662 | yes |

messages.content:
You write the narrative sections of a short research report on an unpublished conjoint experiment, for a reader who knows social science but has not seen the study. You receive the hypotheses with their tags (registered / deviation / exploratory), the result tables, exploratory findings, and a literature note. The report skeleton already prints the model formulas, the full tables, a key-findings table and the figures; your job is the prose around them.

Voice: a careful colleague explaining the study to a peer, not a form being filled in. Vary sentence openings; do not begin the summary and the design notes the same way; do not restate the hypothesis sentence that already sits under each heading; say "significant" once per section at most and otherwise let the interval speak.

Style:
- Plain, legible English. Short paragraphs (2-4 sentences). One idea per sentence. Lead with what was found, then how.
- Refer to arms and outcomes by their labels (e.g. "Automated Flagging", "total accuracy"), never by codes or column names. Do not paste formulas, column names, variable codes or file paths into prose; they are shown separately.
- For an outcome on a 0-1 proportion scale, state effects in percentage points ("4.4 points higher", from +0.044) and give the raw estimate once in parentheses if useful. Give a 95% CI for each effect you name.
- Name the significant effects with their CI and p-value; summarise the rest in one sentence ("the other eight arms were within about ±3 points of control and not distinguishable from it"). Do not list every arm's numbers.
- Numbers must come from the tables. Never add results that are not in the tables.
- A non-significant estimate is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Never write "had no effect", "did not change" or "neither improved nor harmed"; say it was not distinguishable from zero and give the CI.
- Cite the p-value that matches the hypothesis (`p_directional`, one-sided for a stated direction, when present) and say whether it is one- or two-sided, once.
- Mention the sample flow once, in the design notes: raw N, analysis N, and any rows dropped for missing values (`n_eligible` vs model `n`), plus the control-group size.
- If the plan was not pre-registered (registration status "none"), say once, plainly, that every test is post hoc, and never call an analysis "registered" or "pre-specified". If an analysis carries a deviation tag, say in one sentence what changed and why it matters (or does not).
- Exploratory results (E1, E2, ...) come from model-written code that nobody has reviewed. Report them only in their own section and in at most one takeaway, introduced as exploratory. Never let an exploratory result overturn, qualify or cast doubt on a registered result in the abstract or the registered results; if an exploratory check disagrees with a registered estimate, say in the exploratory section that the two disagree and that the check is unreviewed.
- Do not overclaim: p-values near the threshold, small arms and many uncorrected tests all deserve a hedge, stated once.
- No headings, no bullet lists, no bold, no markdown tables inside your sections; plain paragraphs only.

Takeaways: 3 to 5 bullets for a reader who will read nothing else. Each is one or two plain sentences, at most 30 words, with one number at most (the effect in natural units with its CI or p-value). The first bullet answers the research question; the middle ones give the findings that matter, saying "registered" or "exploratory" where it changes the reading; the last gives the main caveat (multiple uncorrected tests, small arms, post hoc). No codes, no column names, no lists of every arm. Every claim names its outcome. Words like "performance", "outcomes" or "anything" are not outcomes. Superlatives ("the only arm to...", "the largest effect") are allowed only for one named outcome and only if the Key numbers block confirms them (bad: "the only registered arm to harm performance"; good: "the only arm that lowered accuracy"). When an effect is negative, write the CI of the effect itself, e.g. −3.9 points (95% CI [−7.4, −0.3]), never a flipped-sign interval. Use the "Key numbers" block for the figures.

Abstract: one paragraph, 120 to 170 words, in the order a journal abstract uses: the question, the design and sample in one sentence, the main results with their numbers, and one sentence of caveat. It must stand alone when shared without the rest of the report.

Length: abstract ≤ 170 words; design_notes ≤ 120 words; each result note ≤ 110 words; each exploratory note ≤ 60 words; limitations ≤ 150 words.

Return ONLY JSON:
{"takeaways": [str, ...], "abstract": str, "design_notes": str, "results": {"H1": str, "H2": str, "S1": str, ...}, "exploratory": {"E1": str, ...}, "limitations": str}

- X1 [exploratory]: A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type. (outcome share, direction two_sided)
- X2 [exploratory]: A1. The slope of plausibility on trust in the sharer, by information type. (outcome plausibility, direction two_sided)

## Literature note
The retrieved list is thin and largely off-topic: none of the ten works reports findings on how information type, tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, political knowledge, or conspiracy belief affect sharing or plausibility judgments of misinformation. The 'supporting' items are broad overviews (Van Bavel et al., 2020; Dwivedi et al., 2019; Jenkins & Purushotma, 2006) with no abstract text bearing on the hypotheses, so they cannot be read as evidence for any of H1-H14. The closest topical neighbors are the conjoint study of deceitful political behavior and political trust [citation removed: not in retrieved set] and the work on political lies and election-loss acceptance (Arceneaux & Truex, 2022). Both concern political deception and trust rather than sharing decisions, so they are context at most. The conjoint design of Christensen et al. (2025) is the only item that resembles the study's method.

The works do not disagree with each other or with the study's expectations on any substantive question about sharing or plausibility. The 'contesting' items (Chater & Loewenstein, 2022, in two versions; Sutton et al., 2010) address individual-level framing of behavioral policy and distributed memory, and they do not test the hypothesized effects. Because no retrieved work reports findings on these questions, the study's design cannot be said to adjudicate between any of them. The abstract for Nativist disidentification (López Ortega & Turnbull-Dugarte, 2025) mentions out-group signals, which is only loosely related to the origin hypotheses (H3, H10), and the snippet is too brief to support a comparison.

## This is a conjoint design
Each hypothesis with arms is one profile feature: the "arms" are its levels and the "control" is its reference level, so each
estimate is an AMCE (the change in the probability that a profile is chosen when the feature takes that level instead of the
reference, averaging over the other features). Write "levels" and "reference level", not "arms" and "control group".
Subgroup tables with columns mm_<group> and difference are differences in marginal means (the share of profiles with that
level that were chosen) between two respondent groups; name the levels whose difference is distinguishable from zero.
design.features marks each feature randomized true/false. Only randomized features have causal AMCEs; for the others say
once, plainly, that they are measured attributes whose AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes, and
never call them randomized. The abstract and takeaways must cover the whole design, not only its largest effect: give the
randomized feature's effects one sentence, then the measured features that matter and the registered subgroup differences
that are distinguishable from zero. Large, expected main effects are not the news when the design was built to study the
other features.

## Hypotheses and subgroups tagged exploratory (ids like X1, XS1)
These were specified by the authors after seeing the data and are estimated by the same deterministic scripts as the
registered tests (not by model-written code). Write a results[<id>] note for each, as for the registered ones, and say once
that they are post hoc. They may appear in at most two takeaways, each introduced as exploratory, and must never qualify a
registered result in the abstract. The pipeline's own exploratory analyses (E1, E2, ...) remain unreviewed model code.

You are the handling editor signing off on a REVISED research report on a conjoint experiment. You receive the revised report, its result tables, and the claims you judged in the previous round (ids C1, C2, ...). Do one thing and return ONLY JSON.

Pressure-test the claims of the revised text. Re-check every previous claim: find its current wording (it may have been reworded or removed) and judge it again against the tables. Then check any new quantitative or causal claim in the Abstract, Key findings and Results prose (at most 12 claims in all, the most consequential first). Verdicts: "supported", "overstated" (true number, too-strong wording or wrong scope), "unsupported" (number or direction not in the tables). A claim that was removed from the text is "supported" with the evidence "removed in revision".

Return:
{"claims": [{"claim": "short quote of the CURRENT wording", "location": "Abstract|Key findings|H1|...", "verdict": "supported|overstated|unsupported", "evidence": "table and row, with the number", "fix": "rewording if not supported, else empty", "previous": "C1 or empty for a new claim", "resolved": true|false}],
 "note": "one sentence for the authors: what, if anything, still needs rewording"}

## Design
A conjoint experiment; causal design: yes; respondents: human.

## Revised report
# Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

*Yamil R. Velez · 2026-10-03 · N = 12,000 analysed of 12,000 collected · conjoint experiment*

<!-- fd:badges -->
![provenance: fully agentic](figures/badges/provenance.svg) ![review: major revision](figures/badges/review.svg) [![plan: pre-registered #132,508](figures/badges/registration.svg)](https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf) ![status: draft](figures/badges/release.svg) ![design: conjoint](figures/badges/design.svg) ![data: open data](figures/badges/data.svg) ![model calls: $0.00](figures/badges/cost.svg)

> **Provenance: FULLY AGENTIC — no human review recorded.** filedrawer 0.1.0, 2026-10-03; orchestrator `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, standard `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`, zero data retention requested. Reviewer pass: yes. Human steps recorded: 0. Release status: draft. Cite as: Velez, Y. R. (2026). Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing [Unpublished study package, generated with filedrawer 0.1.0]. The File Drawer. https://github.com/yrvelez/fact-networks-conjoint

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Of 12,000 profile ratings, 11,882 entered the sharing models; 118 were dropped for missing values, and the report does not break this down by attribute. Each respondent made paired forced choices between two posts, and standard errors are clustered by respondent, not by task. True or neutral headlines (the reference level) contributed 4,145 profiles. Only the headline's information type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes.

### X1. A1. Trust in the sharer → sharing

*A1. Source credibility is conditional on content uncertainty: the slope of sharing on trust in the sharer (1-5), net of the other source attributes, and how it differs by information type.*  
*Exploratory, not pre-registered.*

Slope of Chosen to share on `trust_raw`: 0.014 (SE 0.004, p = 0.000, N = 11882). Significant at alpha = 0.05: yes.

*Exploratory, not pre-registered.*

<!-- fd:section id=abstract -->
## Abstract

We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

<!-- fd:section id=findings -->
## Key findings

- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

<!-- fd:section id=design -->
## Design and data

A conjoint experiment with 7 profile features: randomized, Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); measured rather than randomized (the respondent's own ratings of the real contact each headline was attributed to; only the headline and its assignment to a contact are randomized), Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high); yougov, US. 12,000 responses were collected and 12,000 are analysed. The plan is pre-registered at https://aspredicted.org/8njc-mpqw.pdf. Identifier and free-text columns removed before any model saw the data: none.

![Design at a glance](figures/design.svg)

#### Details: the design in words

A conjoint experiment on yougov respondents in US (N = 12,000 analysed). Each profile is built from 7 features: Information type (True/neutral, Misinformation, Fact-check); Tie strength (Distant tie, Close tie; measured, not randomized); Sharer origin (Foreign origin, Continental US; measured, not randomized); Sharer ideology (Liberal sharer, Moderate sharer, Conservative sharer; measured, not randomized); Trust in sharer (Trust: low, Trust: mid, Trust: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer political knowledge (Knowledge: low, Knowledge: mid, Knowledge: high; measured, not randomized); Sharer belief in disputed claims (Conspiracy belief: low, Conspiracy belief: high; measured, not randomized). Respondents compare two profiles per task and choose one for each outcome. Outcomes: Chosen to share, Chosen as more plausible. Registered moderators: age_t, ideo_self_t, disp_self_t, media_t, survey_language.


The study was registered (AsPredicted #132,508). Of 12,000 profile ratings, 11,882 entered the sharing models; 118 were dropped for missing values, and the report does not break this down by attribute. Each respondent made paired forced choices between two posts, and standard errors are clustered by respondent, not by task. True or neutral headlines (the reference level) contributed 4,145 profiles. Only the headline's information type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. The six sharer traits are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts, so their AMCEs are descriptive contrasts bundling correlated attributes.

## Editor's unresolved questions
- U1: Does contact trust or closeness change sharing when randomized, for instance via randomly assigned sharer profiles, rather than measured on real contacts? (why this study cannot settle it: The traits are respondent ratings of real contacts and are confounded with unmeasured contact characteristics; only a randomized design can separate them.)
- U2: Does misinformation sharing rise with belief in disputed claims in an absolute sense, or only relative to true content, when respondents can decline to share? (why this study cannot settle it: The forced-choice design makes the misinformation increase and the true-content decrease mechanically linked.)
- U3: Do fact-checks reduce sharing equally for health and political claims? (why this study cannot settle it: The topic cells are small (about 1,100 health profiles) and topic was not randomized.)

- Relabel all sharer-trait estimates as conditional associations in the abstract, headings and hypothesis text; reserve 'causal' for the randomized information type.
