You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'mechanism'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
Question: Does a randomly assigned sharer's trustworthiness or closeness change willingness to share a headline?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the design cause: randomizing trust and tie removes confounding with real contact traits, and an opt-out answers U1.
Design sketch: Respondents see single posts, each attributed to a vignette sharer whose relationship (close or distant) and described trustworthiness (low, mid, high) are randomized in a factorial design crossed with information type (true, misinformation, fact-check). The outcome is a 0-100 sharing likelihood plus a 'would not share' option. Quota-sampled US adults answer 8 tasks each, and standard errors are clustered by respondent and task. A subsample also gives a behavioural share-to-feed click.
Power target: about 1500 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed close-tie 0.030 and trust-high 0.057; H2 MDE 0.0258 at n 6709/5256, so about 1,500 per cell clustered detects 0.03.); record it in design.assumptions
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U1

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

Key findings:
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

Limitations: Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's ratings of real contacts, so they are conditional associations that bundle correlated traits. About 14 registered tests and about 180 subgroup contrasts have no multiplicity correction, so results near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer finding, are tentative. Non-significant findings are inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. Several subgroup cells, the low-trust reference cell and the health-headline analyses are small. Standard errors are not clustered by task. The exploratory analyses were specified after seeing the data, and E1 and E2 come from unreviewed code. The sample is a YouGov panel of US adults.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Does contact trust or closeness change sharing when randomized, for instance via randomly assigned sharer profiles, rather than measured on real contacts? (why this study cannot settle it: The traits are respondent ratings of real contacts and are confounded with unmeasured contact characteristics; only a randomized design can separate them.)
- U2: Does misinformation sharing rise with belief in disputed claims in an absolute sense, or only relative to true content, when respondents can decline to share? (why this study cannot settle it: The forced-choice design makes the misinformation increase and the true-content decrease mechanically linked.)
- U3: Do fact-checks reduce sharing equally for health and political claims? (why this study cannot settle it: The topic cells are small (about 1,100 health profiles) and topic was not randomized.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Relabel all sharer-trait estimates as conditional associations in the abstract, headings and hypothesis text; reserve 'causal' for the randomized information type.
- Qualify the moderate-sharer finding as fragile (p=0.034, reweighted p=0.056) or remove it from the abstract.
- State the number of uncorrected tests (about 14 registered plus about 180 subgroup contrasts) next to every highlighted subgroup result, and describe S3 as a mirrored reordering.
- Explain the unit of analysis (paired forced choice), the 118 dropped rows and the E1 sample discrepancy; add a task-clustered robustness fit.
- Discuss E2: the fact-check effect is near zero for health items. Qualify the pooled 13.3-point claim.
- Fix the prose errors: the '−0.0' value, the XS8 reference, the 'about ±2 to 4' interval, and the 'by information type' descriptions that lack interactions.

value.title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
value.rationale: In the source study, close ties (+3.0 points) and high trust (+5.7 points; low-trust cell n=817) were measured on real contacts and bundle correlated traits. Randomly assigning vignette sharers' closeness and trustworthiness, crossed with information type, tests whether these associations survive randomization. A 'would not share' option removes the forced-choice link.
value.contribution: Provides randomized estimates of sharer closeness and trustworthiness effects on sharing across true, false and fact-check content.
limitations: Vignette sharers are hypothetical and may differ from real contacts
Stated sharing likelihood may not match real behaviour; the click is only a subsample proxy
Trust is described rather than experienced
Single-post ratings differ from the source's paired forced choice

design.title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
design.overview: US adults see 8 single posts. Each post is attributed to a vignette sharer whose closeness (close or distant) and trustworthiness (low, mid, high) are randomly assigned, crossed with information type (true, misinformation, fact-check). Respondents rate sharing likelihood on 0-100 or choose 'would not share'. A subsample makes a behavioural share-to-feed click.
design.hypothesis: Randomly assigned close and high-trust sharers raise sharing likelihood relative to distant and low-trust sharers (about 3 points), with effects possibly differing by information type.
design.primaryOutcome: Sharing likelihood (0-100), with a 'would not share' option coded as 0 and analysed separately as a binary outcome.
design.comparison: Close vs distant; trust high and mid vs low; main effects pooled over information type, with exploratory interactions with information type.
design.population: Quota-sampled US adults (age, gender, race, party)

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. ## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'advance_design')
Type: advance_design (survey_experiment). Title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
Question: Does a randomly assigned sharer's trustworthiness or closeness change willingness to share a headline?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the design cause: randomizing trust and tie removes confounding with real contact traits, and an opt-out answers U1.
Design sketch: Respondents see single posts, each attributed to a vignette sharer whose relationship (close or distant) and described trustworthiness (low, mid, high) are randomized in a factorial design crossed with information type (true, misinformation, fact-check). The outcome is a 0-100 sharing likelihood plus a 'would not share' option. Quota-sampled US adults answer 8 tasks each, and standard errors are clustered by respondent and task. A subsample also gives a behavioural share-to-feed click.
Power target: about 1500 per arm to detect 0.03 at 80% power (Observed close-tie 0.030 and trust-high 0.057; H2 MDE 0.0258 at n 6709/5256, so about 1,500 per cell clustered detects 0.03.); record it in design.assumptions

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

Key findings:
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

Limitations: Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's ratings of real contacts, so they are conditional associations that bundle correlated traits. About 14 registered tests and about 180 subgroup contrasts have no multiplicity correction, so results near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer finding, are tentative. Non-significant findings are inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. Several subgroup cells, the low-trust reference cell and the health-headline analyses are small. Standard errors are not clustered by task. The exploratory analyses were specified after seeing the data, and E1 and E2 come from unreviewed code. The sample is a YouGov panel of US adults.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Does contact trust or closeness change sharing when randomized, for instance via randomly assigned sharer profiles, rather than measured on real contacts? (why this study cannot settle it: The traits are respondent ratings of real contacts and are confounded with unmeasured contact characteristics; only a randomized design can separate them.)
- U2: Does misinformation sharing rise with belief in disputed claims in an absolute sense, or only relative to true content, when respondents can decline to share? (why this study cannot settle it: The forced-choice design makes the misinformation increase and the true-content decrease mechanically linked.)
- U3: Do fact-checks reduce sharing equally for health and political claims? (why this study cannot settle it: The topic cells are small (about 1,100 health profiles) and topic was not randomized.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Relabel all sharer-trait estimates as conditional associations in the abstract, headings and hypothesis text; reserve 'causal' for the randomized information type.
- Qualify the moderate-sharer finding as fragile (p=0.034, reweighted p=0.056) or remove it from the abstract.
- State the number of uncorrected tests (about 14 registered plus about 180 subgroup contrasts) next to every highlighted subgroup result, and describe S3 as a mirrored reordering.
- Explain the unit of analysis (paired forced choice), the 118 dropped rows and the E1 sample discrepancy; add a task-clustered robustness fit.
- Discuss E2: the fact-check effect is near zero for health items. Qualify the pooled 13.3-point claim.
- Fix the prose errors: the '−0.0' value, the XS8 reference, the 'about ±2 to 4' interval, and the 'by information type' descriptions that lack interactions.

value.title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
value.rationale: In the source study, close ties (+3.0 points) and high trust (+5.7 points; low-trust cell n=817) were measured on real contacts and bundle correlated traits. Randomly assigning vignette sharers' closeness and trustworthiness tests whether these associations survive randomization. A 'would not share' option removes the forced-choice link.
value.contribution: Provides randomized estimates of sharer closeness and trustworthiness effects on sharing across true, false and fact-check content.
limitations: Vignette sharers are hypothetical and may differ from real contacts
Stated sharing likelihood may not match real behaviour; the click is only a subsample proxy
Trust is described rather than experienced
Single-post ratings differ from the source's paired forced choice
The compact instrument shows one profile per respondent; the full run randomizes per task

design.title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
design.overview: US adults see 8 single posts. Each post is attributed to a vignette sharer whose closeness (close or distant) and trustworthiness (low, high; mid added in the full run) are randomly assigned, crossed with information type (true, misinformation, fact-check). Respondents give a 0-100 sharing likelihood or choose 'would not share'. A subsample makes a behavioural share-to-feed click.
design.hypothesis: Randomly assigned close and high-trust sharers raise sharing likelihood relative to distant and low-trust sharers (about 3 points), with effects possibly differing by information type.
design.primaryOutcome: Sharing likelihood (0-100), with 'would not share' analysed separately as a binary outcome.
design.comparison: Close vs distant; high vs low trust; main effects pooled over information type, with exploratory interactions with information type.
design.population: Quota-sampled US adults (age, gender, race, party)

The person who shared the next post is a close contact, someone you discuss important matters with. People describe them as very trustworthy. Post: {{ed:post_ch}}

Would you choose not to share this post at all?
The person who shared the next post is a close contact, someone you discuss important matters with. People describe them as not very trustworthy. Post: {{ed:post_cl}}
How likely are you to share this post? Enter a number from 0 (not at all) to 100 (certainly).

How likely are you to share this post? Enter a number from 0 (not at all) to 100 (certainly).
Would you choose not to share this post at all?

How likely are you to share this post? Enter a number from 0 (not at all) to 100 (certainly).
Would you choose not to share this post at all?
Would you like to add the last post to a practice feed that we will show to other participants?
Thank you. The sharers were fictional and some posts were false or corrections. Please do not rely on any false claims you saw.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],
 "design": {"title", "overview", "hypothesis", "primaryOutcome", "comparison", "population", "conditions": [{"id","title","description","nodeId"}], "blocks": [{"id","title","questions": [Question]}], "flow": [FlowNode], "roots": [ids], "assumptions": [str], "unresolved": [str], "evidence": [{"id","title","url","claim","excerpt","origin": "supplied"}]}}

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'boundary'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'generalizability_conditional')
Type: generalizability_conditional (survey_experiment). Title: Fact-check effect by topic
Question: Does the fact-check sharing penalty hold for health claims as it does for political claims?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the sample cause: randomizing topic with adequate health items answers U3.
Design sketch: Cross information type (true, misinformation, fact-check) with randomized topic (health, political) over a balanced item bank of at least 20 items per topic. Outcome is sharing choice with an opt-out. Sample US adults with oversampled Spanish-language respondents, given the S5 language differences.
Moderator or condition whose variation the design must cover: Topic (health versus political), and survey language as a secondary condition
Power target: about 1200 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (E2 health fact-check -0.028 (SE 0.028) versus political -0.151; difference of about 0.12 is detectable, but 0.04 targets a smaller health effect; MDE 0.031 at n~4,000 per arm.); record it in design.assumptions
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U3

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

Key findings:
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

Limitations: Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's ratings of real contacts, so they are conditional associations that bundle correlated traits. About 14 registered tests and about 180 subgroup contrasts have no multiplicity correction, so results near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer finding, are tentative. Non-significant findings are inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. Several subgroup cells, the low-trust reference cell and the health-headline analyses are small. Standard errors are not clustered by task. The exploratory analyses were specified after seeing the data, and E1 and E2 come from unreviewed code. The sample is a YouGov panel of US adults.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Does contact trust or closeness change sharing when randomized, for instance via randomly assigned sharer profiles, rather than measured on real contacts? (why this study cannot settle it: The traits are respondent ratings of real contacts and are confounded with unmeasured contact characteristics; only a randomized design can separate them.)
- U2: Does misinformation sharing rise with belief in disputed claims in an absolute sense, or only relative to true content, when respondents can decline to share? (why this study cannot settle it: The forced-choice design makes the misinformation increase and the true-content decrease mechanically linked.)
- U3: Do fact-checks reduce sharing equally for health and political claims? (why this study cannot settle it: The topic cells are small (about 1,100 health profiles) and topic was not randomized.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Relabel all sharer-trait estimates as conditional associations in the abstract, headings and hypothesis text; reserve 'causal' for the randomized information type.
- Qualify the moderate-sharer finding as fragile (p=0.034, reweighted p=0.056) or remove it from the abstract.
- State the number of uncorrected tests (about 14 registered plus about 180 subgroup contrasts) next to every highlighted subgroup result, and describe S3 as a mirrored reordering.
- Explain the unit of analysis (paired forced choice), the 118 dropped rows and the E1 sample discrepancy; add a task-clustered robustness fit.
- Discuss E2: the fact-check effect is near zero for health items. Qualify the pooled 13.3-point claim.
- Fix the prose errors: the '−0.0' value, the XS8 reference, the 'about ±2 to 4' interval, and the 'by information type' descriptions that lack interactions.

## Extensions already written (make yours distinct)
- mechanism: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness — Randomly assigned close and high-trust sharers raise sharing likelihood relative to distant and low-trust sharers (about 3 points), with effects possibly differing by information type.

value.title: Fact-check effect by topic
value.rationale: In the source study fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, but E2 shows the health estimate near zero (-0.028, SE 0.028) against about -0.15 for political items, with only about 1,100 health profiles and topic not randomized. Randomizing topic with a balanced item bank tests whether the penalty really differs by topic, and survey language is added because of language differences.
value.contribution: Provides a randomized, adequately powered test of whether the fact-check sharing penalty holds for health as for political claims, in English and Spanish.
limitations: Single-post sharing with an opt-out differs from the forced-pair choice of the source study.
Item content differs between topics even in a balanced bank; topic effects may reflect item features.
Spanish-language respondents are self-selected into language and language is not randomized.
Hypothetical sharing, not behavior on a platform.

design.title: Fact-check sharing penalty: health versus political claims
design.overview: US adults, with Spanish-language respondents oversampled, are randomized to a topic (health or political). Each sees several posts from a bank of at least 20 items per topic, each shown as true/neutral, misinformation, or fact-check, and chooses whether to share or not share.
design.hypothesis: The fact-check sharing penalty relative to true/neutral posts is smaller for health than for political items. Misinformation is shared less than true content in both topics. Exploratory: the topic difference varies by survey language.
design.primaryOutcome: Share choice for each post (share vs. do not share), with an opt-out.
design.comparison: Fact-check versus true/neutral sharing, compared between health and political topic arms; information type varies within respondent.
design.population: US adults 18+ recruited from an online panel, with Spanish-language respondents oversampled; survey offered in English or Spanish.

messages.content:
You design ONE follow-up survey experiment that extends a finished study. You see the study's abstract, key results and limitations, its design, and the questions of its original survey. You never see respondent data.

Hand the design over with record_result(key="proposal", value=<object>, final=true). Do not write prose outside the object.

The object is an ExtensionProposal:
{"id": the kind given in the task, "kind": "mechanism"|"boundary"|"alternative", "addresses": [ids of unresolved reviewer questions this design answers, e.g. "U1"; may be empty], "title": str, "rationale": 2-3 sentences tying the extension to a specific result or limitation of the source study (cite numbers from the results), "contribution": one sentence, "limitations": [str],

Kinds: "mechanism" tests WHY the source effect (or null) happened; "boundary" tests WHERE it holds (a population, stimulus or context the source did not cover); "alternative" tests a rival explanation or a different intervention for the same outcome.

Design rules (they are checked by a validator; violations are sent back to you):
Produce a complete, concise standalone English survey experiment using the exact schema. Every collecting question needs a unique readable tag. IDs start with letters and contain letters/numbers/underscores. MC choices have stable local IDs, text, numeric recode strings. Matrix rows are statements and choices are scale points. Use empty arrays/strings for irrelevant fields. DB is participant-facing descriptive text. Do not include executable HTML or code. Flow is a flat list with unique IDs, and "roots" lists the top-level node ids in order; child references form a tree. block nodes reference blocks; group nodes contain sequences; randomizer nodes select exactly one equally allocated child arm. Group each arm with an embedded field recording the condition plus its treatment block: randomizer r1 has children [arm_a, arm_b]; arm_a is a group whose children are [set_a, treat_a]; set_a is an embedded node with field "condition" and value "a"; treat_a is a block node. Each condition's nodeId is the group (arm_a), never the embedded node, the block, or the randomizer. block, embedded and end nodes have empty children. A branch after consent is a sibling of the consent block, not its child. Every FlowNode has all fields: id, type, label, children, blockId, field, value, questionId, choiceId, operator ("equals" when unused); unused string fields are "". Every Question has all fields: id, type, text, tag, multiple, required, choices, rows, sourceQuestionId. Ask consent before treatment and route non-consent to an end node through a branch on the consent MC question (operator "selected"). The full instrument includes consent, every treatment, the outcome measures and a debrief. Stimuli that are media live in an embedded node piped into a DB question with {{ed:field}}: [IMAGE: what the image shows] for a still image, [VIDEO: what the clip shows and its length] for a clip the research team hosts. Use one embedded node per stimulus (field names like post1, post2); the DB question text pipes it, e.g. "{{ed:post1}}", and the outcome question for that post follows it. Every {{ed:field}} used in question text must be set by an embedded node earlier in the flow. NEVER put [RESEARCHER INPUT REQUIRED], TBD, TODO or placeholders in question text: the validator rejects the whole design. Anything only the research team can supply (the actual media files, IRB numbers, compensation) goes in design.unresolved as a plain sentence, and the participant wording stays complete. Record practical judgment calls (sample size with rationale, platform, compensation) in design.assumptions.

Grounding rules:
- Reuse the source survey's outcome questions verbatim where they fit, with sourceQuestionId set to their QSF id (e.g. "QID12"); use "" for new questions. Only ids listed under "Source survey questions" are valid.
- evidence: cite only the allowed sources listed in the task, by their exact url; origin "supplied"; excerpt may be "".
- Two to four arms. Keep it short enough for a 10-minute survey.

Write the 'alternative'-type extension specified in the brief below.

## Brief (design exactly this; use id 'theoretical_debate')
Type: theoretical_debate (survey_experiment). Title: Absolute versus relative misinformation sharing by belief
Question: Do respondents who believe more disputed claims share more misinformation in absolute terms, or only relatively against true content?
Why this follow-up fixes what held the source study back: Fixes the measurement cause: single-item rating with an opt-out breaks the forced-choice link and answers U2.
Design sketch: Randomize format between paired forced choice (replication) and independent single-headline sharing with a 'share nothing' option. Information type is randomized within respondent, and belief in disputed claims is measured pre-treatment. Compare the belief by information-type slope across formats. If the slope for misinformation survives in single-item format, the effect is absolute.
Power target: about 1800 per arm to detect 0.04 at 80% power (S3 differences of 0.055 to 0.056 with SE 0.017; the interaction across formats needs about double the cell size.); record it in design.assumptions
Reviewer questions it answers (set "addresses" to these): U2

## Source study
Title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing

Abstract: We ask how the type of information and the characteristics of the person who shares it relate to whether people choose to share a post and whether they judge it plausible. In a registered conjoint experiment with 12,000 YouGov profile ratings in the US, headlines (true or neutral, false, or a fact-check) were randomly attributed to real contacts named by respondents, whose traits were measured. Misinformation was chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral content (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]); fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) were associated with higher sharing. The information-type pattern replicated for plausibility, but trust did not. Sharer traits are measured, so these are conditional associations, and about 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts were uncorrected.

Key findings:
- Misinformation headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]). Fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, driven by political items; the health estimate is near zero.
- High trust in the sharer was associated with 5.7 points more sharing (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]) and a close tie with 3.0 points more (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]). These are measured contrasts, and the low-trust reference cell is thin.
- Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±1.7 to ±2.2 points. Trust did not carry over to plausibility.
- Respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (−5.5 points). This is a relative reordering, one of about 180 uncorrected subgroup contrasts.
- Only information type is randomized; sharer traits are measured associations. About 14 registered tests plus about 180 subgroup contrasts are uncorrected, so results near p=0.05 are tentative.

Limitations: Only the headline type and its assignment to a contact are randomized. Tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's ratings of real contacts, so they are conditional associations that bundle correlated traits. About 14 registered tests and about 180 subgroup contrasts have no multiplicity correction, so results near the threshold, such as the moderate-sharer finding, are tentative. Non-significant findings are inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect. Several subgroup cells, the low-trust reference cell and the health-headline analyses are small. Standard errors are not clustered by task. The exploratory analyses were specified after seeing the data, and E1 and E2 come from unreviewed code. The sample is a YouGov panel of US adults.

## Questions the reviewers raised that this study cannot settle (prefer a design that answers one; list its id in "addresses")
- U1: Does contact trust or closeness change sharing when randomized, for instance via randomly assigned sharer profiles, rather than measured on real contacts? (why this study cannot settle it: The traits are respondent ratings of real contacts and are confounded with unmeasured contact characteristics; only a randomized design can separate them.)
- U2: Does misinformation sharing rise with belief in disputed claims in an absolute sense, or only relative to true content, when respondents can decline to share? (why this study cannot settle it: The forced-choice design makes the misinformation increase and the true-content decrease mechanically linked.)
- U3: Do fact-checks reduce sharing equally for health and political claims? (why this study cannot settle it: The topic cells are small (about 1,100 health profiles) and topic was not randomized.)

## The review editor's guidance on this study (avoid repeating its weaknesses)
- Relabel all sharer-trait estimates as conditional associations in the abstract, headings and hypothesis text; reserve 'causal' for the randomized information type.
- Qualify the moderate-sharer finding as fragile (p=0.034, reweighted p=0.056) or remove it from the abstract.
- State the number of uncorrected tests (about 14 registered plus about 180 subgroup contrasts) next to every highlighted subgroup result, and describe S3 as a mirrored reordering.
- Explain the unit of analysis (paired forced choice), the 118 dropped rows and the E1 sample discrepancy; add a task-clustered robustness fit.
- Discuss E2: the fact-check effect is near zero for health items. Qualify the pooled 13.3-point claim.
- Fix the prose errors: the '−0.0' value, the XS8 reference, the 'about ±2 to 4' interval, and the 'by information type' descriptions that lack interactions.

## Extensions already written (make yours distinct)
- mechanism: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness — Randomly assigned close and high-trust sharers raise sharing likelihood relative to distant and low-trust sharers (about 3 points), with effects possibly differing by information type.
- boundary: Fact-check effect by topic — The fact-check sharing penalty relative to true/neutral posts is smaller for health than for political items. Misinformation is shared less than true content in both topics. Exploratory: the topic difference varies by survey language.

value.title: Absolute versus relative misinformation sharing by belief
value.rationale: In the source study, respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (-5.5 points), a mirrored pattern that forced choice makes mechanically linked. Belief in disputed claims had no distinguishable overall effect on sharing (intervals about ±1.7 to 2.2 points). Independent single-headline sharing with a 'share nothing' option tests whether the belief slope for misinformation is absolute.
value.contribution: Separates absolute from relative belief-related misinformation sharing by breaking the forced-choice link between misinformation and true items.
limitations: Headline stimuli differ from the real-contact framing of the source study.
Belief is measured pre-treatment and may prime respondents.
Cross-format interaction needs about double the cell size.

design.title: Paired forced choice versus single-headline sharing by belief in disputed claims
design.overview: Respondents first rate belief in disputed claims. They are randomized to a paired forced-choice format (replication) or an independent single-headline format with a 'share nothing' option. Within respondent, each sees true/neutral and false headlines.
design.hypothesis: In forced choice, belief in disputed claims predicts more misinformation and less true-content choice (mirrored). In single-item format, if the belief slope for misinformation sharing remains positive, the effect is absolute; if it is near zero while the true-content slope is negative or null, it is purely relative.
design.primaryOutcome: Share of misinformation headlines shared (single format) or chosen (forced choice), by belief index.
design.comparison: Belief by information-type slope compared across formats (three-way interaction: format x belief x information type).
design.population: US adults from an online panel such as YouGov, matching the source sample.
